Twitter’s Quest for a Graal Runtime: Devoxx France 2018 Insights

At Devoxx France 2018, Christian Thalinger, a compiler expert at Twitter, delivered a talk titled Twitter’s quest for a wholly Graal runtime. Available on YouTube, the session detailed Twitter’s adoption of the Graal JIT compiler to optimize its massive Java-based infrastructure. With thousands of JVMs running across thousands of machines, Twitter aimed to reduce CPU usage and costs through better machine code generation. Thalinger shared the year-long journey, including challenges, bug fixes, and performance gains, offering a compelling case for Graal’s potential in large-scale systems.

Who Is Christian Thalinger?

Christian Thalinger, a 13-year veteran of JVM compiler development, works on Twitter’s VM team, building a custom JDK to optimize performance. Previously at Sun Microsystems and Oracle, he contributed to the HotSpot JVM’s C2 compiler, added invokedynamic support (JSR 292), and developed JVM Compiler Interface (JVMCI, JSR 243) for JDK 9. Living in Hawaii, Thalinger humorously encouraged the audience to tweet about his talk with the hashtag #TwitterVMTeam, ensuring his colleagues knew he was working, not just relaxing.

Twitter’s Scale and Motivation

Twitter operates a vast distributed system with services like the tweet service, user service, social graph, and timeline service, supported by hundreds of smaller services (e.g., DM, URL, image). These run on thousands of JVM instances across multiple data centers, consuming significant resources. Even small performance improvements, amplified across this scale, yield substantial savings in electricity, cooling, and potentially server count. Thalinger’s goal was clear: use Graal, an open-source JIT compiler, to generate better machine code, reduce CPU utilization, and cut costs.

Understanding Graal and JIT Compilation

Graal is a JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler, written in Java, that translates Java bytecode into native machine code to boost application performance. Unlike HotSpot’s C1 (client) and C2 (server) compilers, Graal offers a modular design and advanced optimizations like improved inlining and escape analysis. Inlining embeds method calls directly into the caller’s code, reducing overhead, while escape analysis eliminates unnecessary object allocations if they don’t escape a method’s scope, reducing garbage collection (GC) overhead.

Thalinger clarified that his talk focused solely on Graal the JIT compiler, not the broader GraalVM project, which includes SubstrateVM and Truffle for multi-language support. Twitter’s services, primarily written in Scala (92% of the tweet service), rely on Java bytecode, making Graal’s optimizations particularly effective due to Scala’s polymorphic and complex bytecode.

Why Replace C2 with Graal?

HotSpot’s C2 compiler, while robust, is aging and complex, with a steep learning curve. Thalinger noted it took him three to four years to master C2, and new developers often struggled, sometimes leaving due to frustration. Recent C2 updates focused on handwritten intrinsics (e.g., for String.indexOf) rather than fundamental improvements. Graal, by contrast, is easier to understand, with a modular package structure and no circular dependencies. Its open-source nature aligns with Twitter’s heavy use of open-source tools, and Twitter contributes back to the Graal project.

The Journey to Graal

Thalinger joined Twitter’s VM team, which maintains a custom JDK based on Java 8, and backported JVMCI (JSR 243) to enable Graal integration. The team ran Graal in tiered compilation mode, where C1 compiles code quickly for initial execution, and Graal optimizes hot methods for peak performance. Over a year, they encountered and fixed several bugs:

  • On-Stack Replacement (OSR) Issue: Graal failed to compile certain methods, throwing exceptions. Initially, Twitter relied on C1 as a fallback, but Oracle’s Leopold fixed it with 1,000 lines of code.
  • Static Field Access: Graal lacked logic to handle static class initializers accessing final fields, causing compilation failures. Twitter added 30 lines of C2-equivalent code to resolve it.
  • Long-Running Process Crash: A crash occurred after days of runtime due to the Heapster agent instrumenting Graal’s Java-based snippets. Oracle’s Doug added 2,700 lines to fix this, critical for agent-using environments.
  • Byte Reversal Bug: A Graal intrinsic for reversing bytes in Short was incorrect, causing Netty buffer failures. A small fix (two lines plus tests) resolved it.

These fixes, contributed upstream, stabilized Graal for Twitter’s production environment.

Performance Results

Thalinger tested Graal on the tweet service, a Finagle-based service (92% Scala), using a dedicated cluster to eliminate crosstalk. Identical requests were sent to JVMs running C2 and Graal on JDK 8 and 9. Key findings:

  • GC Cycles: Graal reduced GC cycles by 2.5%, indicating fewer temporary object allocations due to better escape analysis.
  • CPU Usage: Graal cut user CPU time by 11% in controlled tests, dropping to 8% in production due to real-world factors like write traffic. Disabling escape analysis showed 5% came from inlining improvements, with the rest from escape analysis.
  • Memory Overhead: Graal used 40MB more memory for its Java-based state, a fixed cost regardless of heap size, deemed negligible.

Further tuning of Graal’s inlining parameters one afternoon yielded an additional 1.3–1.5% reduction in GC cycles and 2% in CPU time, amplifying savings. Thalinger estimated that for a hypothetical company with 10,000 servers (24 cores each) at $127 per core annually, an 11% CPU reduction saves $330,000 yearly. Twitter, with over 10,000 servers, likely saves more.

Scala’s Role in Gains

Scala’s complex, polymorphic bytecode benefits significantly from Graal’s inlining, explaining the 11% improvement. Java code, being more straightforward, may see smaller or no gains, though some Java benchmarks showed up to 10% improvement. Thalinger expressed interest in testing Kotlin but hadn’t yet, encouraging community experiments.

Graal’s Broader Impact

Graal is included in JDK 9+ as an experimental compiler via JVMCI, used in ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation (JSR 295). Twitter runs Graal in production for services like tweet, user, and social graph, with plans to convert all services. Thalinger urged developers to try Graal, report bugs, and help mature it, as Twitter did. Oracle’s Project Metropolis aims to replace C2 and other HotSpot components (e.g., bytecode verifier) with Java-based versions, potentially leveraging Graal.

Why It Matters

Thalinger’s talk highlights Graal’s potential to modernize JVM performance, especially for Scala-heavy systems like Twitter’s. The 8–11% CPU reduction translates to millions in savings at scale, while Graal’s modular design ensures maintainability. By sharing bug fixes and encouraging adoption, Twitter contributes to a more efficient, open-source Java ecosystem. Developers can explore Graal via JDK 9+ or GraalVM, testing it to uncover further optimizations. This session inspires innovation in performance-critical applications, proving small changes can yield big rewards.

Debugging Microservices in Kubernetes: Devoxx France 2018 Insights

At Devoxx France 2018, Ray Tsang (Google Cloud) and Baruch Sadogursky (JFrog) presented a session titled Troubleshooting & Debugging Production Microservices in Kubernetes. Available on YouTube, the talk used a live demo to showcase tools for diagnosing issues in a Kubernetes-deployed microservices application. Simulating a failing guestbook app, they demonstrated Kubernetes-native tools, Weave Scope, JFrog Artifactory, and Google’s Stackdriver to trace errors, emphasizing observability and best practices for production debugging.

Who Are Ray Tsang and Baruch Sadogursky?

Ray Tsang, a developer advocate for Google Cloud Platform, promotes technologies like Kubernetes and gRPC. Baruch Sadogursky, a developer advocate at JFrog, focuses on tools like Artifactory for artifact management. Their engaging, humorous presentation—complete with “good cop, bad cop” banter—guided the audience through a practical debugging scenario, urging attendees to follow them on Twitter (@saturnism, @jbaruch) and visit a landing page (jfrog.com/au) for resources.

The Guestbook App and Its Failure

The presenters introduced a guestbook application, a simple Java-based Spring app allowing users to submit names and messages, combining “hello world” and database persistence. Designed as a microservices architecture, it included a frontend UI, two backend services (hello-world and guestbook), MySQL for data storage, and Redis for session replication. Each screen element was a microservice, requiring extensive YAML configurations for Kubernetes deployment on a five-machine Google Cloud cluster.

The demo began with a failure: the app returned a 404 error, with no clear error message. This set the stage for a detective-style investigation, mimicking real-world production issues where vague errors demand systematic troubleshooting.

Step 1: Verify the Docker Image

Tsang and Sadogursky started by checking the Docker image in the UI deployment. Using kubectl describe, they confirmed the image was from JFrog Artifactory, tagged as latest. However, latest lacked version specificity, prompting a search in Artifactory. The image’s SHA-256 fingerprint identified it as version 50, and the Dockerfile showed a copied JAR file—also tagged latest. The build metadata, linked to a Jenkins pipeline, revealed no suspicious changes or new dependencies, ruling out a faulty build.

Step 2: Compare Staging and Production

To isolate the issue, they checked the staging environment, a Kubernetes namespace replicating production. The staging app worked, displaying the guestbook. Comparing Docker image fingerprints confirmed staging and production used the same version 50, suggesting the issue wasn’t the image itself but an environmental or runtime factor.

Step 3: Inspect Logs

With the image verified, they turned to logs. Using kubectl logs --follow, they streamed logs from a UI instance but found no clear error due to the app’s microservices complexity. To handle multiple instances, they suggested tools like kubetail, which aggregates logs from all pods in a deployment. However, rapid log scrolling in production can obscure errors, so they recommended centralized logging.

On Google Cloud, Stackdriver Logging captures stdout and stderr outputs from containers, avoiding ephemeral filesystem issues. Querying Stackdriver revealed a 404 error from an HTTP client, but no specific cause. A BigQuery export allowed structured queries, showing two instances had significantly more errors (hundreds vs. seven in others). This suggested an instance-specific issue.

Step 4: Isolate and Interrogate

Rather than restarting the faulty instance, they isolated it to avoid losing diagnostic data. Kubernetes labels were key: each pod had a serving: true label, matched by the load balancer. By updating one instance’s label to serving: false via kubectl, they removed it from service without affecting the deployment’s scale (Kubernetes automatically launched a replacement). A kubectl port-forward connected their local machine to the isolated instance, confirming the same 404 error, indicating the issue persisted.

Step 5: Enhance Observability with Weave Scope and Zipkin

To map service interactions, they used Weave Scope, which visualizes Kubernetes pods and connections. However, its lines were based on deployment annotations, risking outdated documentation. For real-time observability, they turned to Zipkin, which traces requests across microservices using trace IDs. Zipkin revealed a 500 error from the hello-world service’s /hello endpoint, not the UI, pinpointing the root cause: a 404 bubbled up as a 500 due to poor error handling.

Step 6: Dynamic Debugging with Stackdriver Debugger

To investigate without redeploying, they used Stackdriver Debugger, which attaches JVM agents to running applications. Without modifying class files, they added a log statement to print the name variable in the hello-world service. The logs showed an empty name, revealing a null pointer issue due to a cached session. Adding a null check via the debugger (safely, as it blocks state-modifying expressions) confirmed the user error. The fix—clearing the session or adding input validation—could be applied later.

Best Practices and Tools

The presenters emphasized observability: centralized logging (Stackdriver, ELK), distributed tracing (Zipkin, Jaeger), and live debugging (Stackdriver Debugger). Kubernetes’ label-based isolation and auto-scaling ensure minimal disruption. Artifactory’s build metadata provides traceability, while avoiding latest tags ensures reproducibility. These tools, many usable outside Google Cloud, streamline production debugging, reducing downtime and manual effort.

Why It Matters

Tsang and Sadogursky’s session demystifies debugging complex microservices in Kubernetes, offering a practical workflow for production issues. By simulating a failure, they showcased tools like Stackdriver, Zipkin, and Artifactory, applicable to any Kubernetes environment. The emphasis on observability, traceability, and non-disruptive debugging empowers developers to resolve issues quickly, enhancing system reliability. This talk equips teams to tackle real-world challenges, ensuring robust, scalable microservices deployments.

The Anatomy of Java Vulnerabilities: Devoxx France 2018 Insights

At Devoxx France 2018, Steve Poole, a Java veteran from IBM, delivered a talk titled The Anatomy of Java Vulnerabilities. Available on YouTube, the session explored why Java, running on billions of devices, is a prime target for cyberattacks. Poole dissected vulnerabilities, their exploits, and the growing threat of cybercrime, urging developers to take responsibility for securing their code. With real-world examples and code snippets, he provided practical insights into reducing security risks in Java applications.

Who Is Steve Poole?

Steve Poole has worked on Java Virtual Machine (JVM) development since its pre-1.0 days, contributing to IBM’s Java team. After a brief stint leading a DevOps team, he returned to Java with a heightened focus on security, informed by real-world challenges. His engaging, candid style—joking about proving to his boss he wasn’t just “drinking wine” at the conference—set the stage for a sobering look at Java’s vulnerabilities. Poole aimed to leave developers “slightly better informed but a lot more worried.”

Why Java Is a Target

Java’s ubiquity—powering servers, clients, and billions of devices—makes it a magnet for malware. While Java applets were historically risky, server-side Java is equally vulnerable. Poole highlighted a 2001 bug in Double.parseDouble, where a specific string (e.g., a large floating-point number) caused threads to hang. This obscure flaw became exploitable when attackers embedded it in HTTP Accept headers, which accept floating-point values per the BNF spec. A simple curl command could flood a server, causing denial-of-service (DoS) by hanging threads repeatedly. This bug, fixed with a two-character code change, cost millions to patch across JVMs and app servers.

What Is a Vulnerability?

A vulnerability is a bug with an exploit—code that attackers use to cause harm, such as DoS, data theft, code execution, or privilege escalation. Poole emphasized that vulnerabilities are often simple. For example, a URL decoding error in a file path check allowed attackers to create files in Windows root directories or Java classpaths. If a non-existent classpath directory was created with malicious code, the next application run could execute it, compromising the system. This flaw, stemming from a single line of code, exposed how small oversights enable big attacks.

The Scale of Cybercrime

Poole underscored the organized nature of cybercrime, dispelling the stereotype of lone hackers. In 2016, cybercrime generated $450 billion globally, surpassing the $435 billion drug trade. By 2021, it was projected to reach $6 trillion annually—equivalent to €600 per person worldwide. Unlike drug trafficking, cybercrime carries low risk of prosecution, fueling its growth. Attackers, as educated as developers, attend conferences to study systems, exploiting APIs and code weaknesses. This arms race pits “white hat” defenders against “black hat” attackers scanning for vulnerabilities.

Attack Vectors and Exploits

Poole outlined key attack vectors:

  • Data Validation Failures: Unchecked inputs, like oversized images or malicious JPEGs, can crash systems or execute arbitrary code. A JPEG parsing bug in C code allowed hidden payloads to run during image processing.
  • Apache Struts Flaw: In the Equifax breach, invalid Content-Type headers containing OGNL scripts were executed during error handling, exposing sensitive data. This showed how “helpful” error messages can backfire.
  • Untrusted Code: Attackers invoke existing system code, like legacy applets or plugins, to gain access. Weak cryptographic protocols or implementation bugs also create openings.
  • Local System Attacks: Ransomware like WannaCry exploited payload delivery to compromise machines, earning attackers $85,000 while disrupting hospitals and production lines.

Developer Responsibility

Developers often dismiss security as an ops issue, but Poole argued they’re prime targets for social engineering. Their elevated privileges, trust in open-source code, and tendency to disable security checks (e.g., SSL validation) make them vulnerable. A GitHub search for TrustManager implementations revealed 100,000 instances of overly permissive code, shared publicly and exploitable. Features like custom error messages or debug protocols (e.g., JDWP) expose system details, aiding attackers. Poole cited a bank hacked via exposed JDWP ports, granting full memory access.

A Real-World Example

Poole presented a code snippet where a Properties object loaded classes dynamically based on input. A default handler loaded FooDrinkHandler, but an attacker could input java.ext.dirs, dumping extension directory contents. This exposed classpath details, enabling targeted attacks like WannaCry-style code injection. Such “developer aids”—designed for convenience—become exploitable when they leak information or trust unvalidated inputs.

Managing Vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are tracked via Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) databases, like MITRE’s CVE List. In 2018, 1,761 CVEs mentioned Java, though all languages have bugs. Details are often “unspecified” to avoid aiding attackers, akin to not tweeting a credit card PIN. CVEs are scored based on exploit likelihood, impact (availability, integrity, confidentiality), and time-sensitive factors. Oracle and IBM issue advisories, but developers must apply fixes. Out-of-band patches signal critical issues requiring immediate action.

Practical Steps for Developers

Poole urged developers to:

  • Validate Inputs: Check all data, including text, images, and binary formats, to prevent exploits.
  • Avoid Custom Security: Don’t write custom TrustManager or parsers; use community-vetted libraries.
  • Update Dependencies: Regularly patch code and libraries, as outdated versions are known targets.
  • Limit Information Leakage: Avoid detailed error messages or stack traces in production (e.g., custom 404 pages).
  • Learn Secure Coding: Study Oracle’s Secure Coding Guidelines and CWE’s Seven Pernicious Kingdoms for anti-patterns.
  • Use Tools: Tools like FindBugs, SonarQube, or OWASP’s dependency checkers scan for vulnerabilities.
  • Explore Serialization Risks: IBM’s serialization guide details safer designs.
  • Consider Microservices: They isolate breaches, limiting damage.

Why It Matters

Poole’s talk is a wake-up call for Java developers. Cybercrime’s scale—outpacing the drug trade—demands proactive defense. Simple bugs, like a parsing flaw or unvalidated input, can cripple systems or leak data. By adopting secure coding practices, validating inputs, and staying vigilant, developers can reduce risks. The session inspires action, encouraging exploration of CVE databases, secure coding resources, and penetration testing to fortify Java applications against an ever-evolving threat landscape.

Mastering Functional Programming: Devoxx France 2018 Insights

At Devoxx France 2018, Xavier Détant, from Zenika, delivered a talk titled Tout ce que vous avez toujours voulu savoir sur la programmation fonctionnelle. Available on YouTube, the session demystified functional programming (FP) through a live-coding exercise in JavaScript. Refactoring an imperative DVD search program into a functional one, Détant introduced key FP concepts with clarity, making them accessible to all. The talk highlighted why FP matters in modern computing, especially for parallelization, and encouraged exploring pure FP languages like Haskell.

Who Is Xavier Détant?

Xavier Détant, a developer at Zenika, used his expertise to break down complex FP concepts in a relatable way. Choosing JavaScript for its familiarity, he tackled a simple problem: searching a DVD collection by title (e.g., finding “Matrix” or films starting with “I”). His live-coding approach, paired with humor and continuous test feedback, kept the audience engaged. Détant’s goal was to make FP approachable, showing how its principles apply to everyday coding challenges.

The Imperative Starting Point

The initial program was a classic imperative solution: a findByTitle function looped through a movie array, checking if the search string was in each title using includes, and pushed matches to a result array. Tests confirmed it worked—finding “Matrix,” returning an empty array for “Interstellar,” and matching “I” to “Intouchable” and “Forrest Gump.” However, Détant noted its flaws: imperative code dictates how to compute, not what to compute, and side effects (like modifying arrays) make reasoning harder.

Refactoring Journey

Détant began refactoring to reduce side effects, a core FP principle. An early test refactor introduced a shared movies array, but a bug emerged: the original code used collection.shift(), removing the first element, causing later tests to fail. Switching to for...of fixed this, illustrating how side effects break predictability. This led to the first FP lesson: minimize side effects, confining them to the program’s “periphery” (e.g., I/O), as pure functions ease reasoning and testing.

Key Functional Concepts

Through iterative refactoring, Détant introduced FP concepts, each tied to the code:

  • First-Class Functions: Assigning the match function to a predicate variable showed functions are values, like arrays. This enabled passing predicate to a renamed addIf function, maintaining test passes.
  • Closures: Moving the side-effecting result.push into a function that accessed result from its outer scope created a closure. This function, passed to addIf, encapsulated result without exposing it.
  • Higher-Order Functions: addIf became a higher-order function, accepting and returning functions. It returned a function to push movies, deferring side effects to the caller.
  • Lambda Calculus: Anonymous functions (lambdas) replaced named ones, aligning with lambda calculus, the mathematical foundation of FP. JavaScript’s arrow syntax (=>) simplified this.
  • Currying: Transforming add (taking movie and movies) into a function taking movie and returning a function for movies enabled currying. This allowed partial application—passing movie early to get a function awaiting movies.
  • Partial Application: Applying match with a search string created a predicate for filter, reducing duplication.
  • Point-Free Notation: Using JavaScript’s filter and includes eliminated explicit loops, focusing on what (filter movies) not how (loop and push).

Eliminating Side Effects

The final refactor replaced addIf with JavaScript’s filter, removing side effects entirely. Instead of pushing to result, filter returned a new array of matches. includes replaced isInfixOf, and title extracted movie titles. The code became concise, functional, and pure—inputs mapped to outputs without modifying state. Tests still passed, proving the behavior was unchanged but safer and clearer.

Functional Programming’s Relevance

Détant connected FP to modern computing challenges. The end of Moore’s Law—where processor speed doubled every 18 months—shifted performance gains to multi-core systems. Parallelization, critical for leveraging multiple cores, is complex with side effects but straightforward in FP. Pure functions, being referentially transparent (same inputs, same outputs), are safe for parallel execution. Java’s Stream.parallel() leverages this, but side effects in streams break correctness, reinforcing FP’s value.

Exploring Pure FP with Haskell

To prove the code’s functional purity, Détant ported it to Haskell, a strongly typed, pure FP language. With minor syntax changes (e.g., -> instead of =>, \ for lambdas), the JavaScript code ran in Haskell, passing tests. Haskell’s type system enforced correctness, catching errors like missing findByTitle. Détant recommended learning pure FP languages like Haskell or Elm to grasp FP principles before applying them in hybrid languages like Java, Scala, or Kotlin.

Why It Matters

Détant’s talk makes FP accessible, showing how familiar JavaScript can become functional with simple changes. Concepts like currying, closures, and point-free notation, rooted in lambda calculus, empower developers to write safer, parallelizable code. As multi-core systems dominate, FP’s emphasis on purity and immutability is increasingly vital. The session inspires exploration of Haskell or Elm to master FP, then applying it in hybrid languages for robust, scalable applications.

SSL/TLS for Mortals: Mastering Secure Communication

At Devoxx France 2018, Maarten Mulders delivered a talk titled SSL/TLS for Mortals, demystifying the complexities of secure communication. Available on YouTube, the session tackled why SSL/TLS is challenging for developers, exploring public/private key encryption, certificates, digital signatures, and certificate authorities. Through live demos and a cautionary tale about a Dutch notary, Mulders provided practical tools and insights to help developers confidently handle secure connections. This talk empowers attendees to become “that one colleague” who understands SSL/TLS and troubleshoot effectively.

Who Is Maarten Mulders?

Maarten Mulders, a developer with a non-native French speaker, switched to English for clarity, humorously acknowledging the audience’s effort. His approachable style made SSL/TLS—often left to the “certificate expert”—accessible. Mulders used packet sniffers and command-line tools like curl and openssl to demonstrate real-world scenarios, drawing from his expertise to simplify transport-layer security. His goal was to equip developers with knowledge to secure distributed systems, crucial in an era of cloud-based, cross-data-center communication.

The Need for SSL/TLS Security

Mulders opened with a relatable scenario: who’s seen a stack trace from a failed secure connection? These cryptic errors are hard to diagnose, yet SSL/TLS is vital as systems increasingly communicate across servers, data centers, and public clouds. Unsecured connections risk interception, like banking credentials exposed over public Wi-Fi. Mulders demonstrated this with a packet sniffer on a local web server, showing plaintext HTTP traffic (e.g., “lorem ipsum”) sent via curl. This vulnerability underscores why SSL/TLS, which encrypts data at the transport layer, is essential, saving developers from implementing encryption in every application.

A Brief History of SSL/TLS

Mulders traced SSL/TLS evolution: SSL 1.0 was never released; SSL 2.0 (1995) and 3.0 (1996) were broken by the POODLE and BEAST attacks, respectively. TLS 1.0 (similar to SSL 3.0) is also outdated. By 2018, TLS 1.1 (2006) and 1.2 (2008) were trustworthy, with TLS 1.3 in draft. He warned against using broken protocols, noting issues with Maven Central and older Java versions. This history highlights the importance of staying current to avoid vulnerabilities.

Public/Private Key Encryption

Mulders explained public/private key encryption using an IKEA-style analogy: a safe with two keys—one public (a globe icon, shareable) and one private (with the owner’s face, secret). To send a “love letter,” the sender locks it in the safe using the recipient’s public key; only the recipient’s private key unlocks it. He then outlined the RSA algorithm, selecting prime numbers (e.g., P=11, Q=17, modulo=187) and a random number (E=3) to compute a private key (D=107). Encrypting “G” (value 7) yields 156; decrypting requires P, Q, and D, which are computationally hard to guess without the private key. This ensures secure communication, as long as the private key remains secret.

Establishing a Secure Connection

Mulders detailed the TLS handshake: the client says “hello,” listing supported TLS versions, algorithms, and compression methods. The server responds, selecting compatible options and sending its certificate and public key. The client sends a premaster secret, both compute a session key, and switch to encrypted communication. A demo showed a web server’s encrypted traffic, unreadable to sniffers, unlike the earlier plaintext. This process ensures no eavesdropping, critical for secure data exchange.

Certificates and Signatures

A certificate, like a driver’s license, is a digital document with a serial number, subject, validity period, usage, public key, and fingerprint for integrity. Self-signed certificates are easy to create but untrusted. Mulders used openssl s_client to inspect a self-signed certificate on his server, showing issuer details. Signed certificates require a signature from a certificate authority (CA), calculated using the CA’s private key. The public key verifies the signature, ensuring authenticity. A “bad guy” with a different key can’t forge a valid signature, as the public key won’t unlock it.

Certificate Authorities and Trust

CAs, often commercial entities, certify public key ownership, creating a chain of trust. Mulders illustrated this: he trusts John, who trusts Alice, who trusts an unknown person, establishing trust transitively. Operating systems (e.g., macOS) and JVMs include ~160 trusted CAs, selected by Apple or Oracle. Mulders noted the risk: users inherit these trust decisions. CAs use rigorous “key ceremonies” (160-page procedures, cameras, random auditors) to protect private keys, ensuring trust in the certificates they sign.

The DigiNotar Cautionary Tale

Mulders shared a real-world failure: DigiNotar, a Dutch CA in Beverwijk, was compromised in 2011. An attacker exploited a DotNetNuke 4.8.0 file upload vulnerability and weak Windows passwords, accessing machines signing certificates. This led to 247 certificates being blacklisted by Google, Microsoft, and Mozilla. The Dutch government delayed Microsoft’s update for two weeks, fearing IT infrastructure collapse, as state certificates relied on DigiNotar. The company went bankrupt, highlighting the catastrophic impact of CA breaches. Mulders criticized a Dutch minister’s naive advice to “trust the green checkmark,” emphasizing vigilance.

Practical Tools and Tips

Mulders offered actionable advice:

  • Use curl -v: Verbose logging reveals certificate issues.
  • Use curl -k (with care): Bypasses certificate checks for internal testing.
  • Use openssl s_client: Inspects certificates (e.g., openssl s_client -connect localhost:9001 -showcerts -servername example.com) to verify chains.
  • Java Settings: Set javax.net.ssl.trustStore and trustStorePassword for trusted certificates; use keyStore for client certificates. Enable javax.net.debug=all for detailed TLS logs.
  • Tools: Use keytool for keystore management or Portecle for a GUI alternative.

He addressed audience questions, clarifying why server names are needed (to select the correct certificate on multi-site servers) and noting no known tool simplifies Java’s verbose TLS debug logs.

Why It Matters

Mulders’ talk is a call to action for developers to master SSL/TLS. As distributed systems grow, secure communication is non-negotiable. Understanding public/private keys, certificates, and CAs prevents reliance on “that one colleague.” The DigiNotar case warns of real-world risks, while tools like curl and openssl empower troubleshooting. This session inspires confidence to secure connections, explore CA processes, and stay updated on TLS protocols.

Spring Framework 5: Feature Highlights & Hidden Gems from Devoxx France 2018

At Devoxx France 2018, Juergen Hoeller, Spring Framework project lead, delivered a talk titled Spring Framework 5 Feature Highlights & Hidden Gems. Available on YouTube, the session explored Spring Framework 5’s major features, focusing on functional and reactive programming, Java 8+ baseline, and lesser-known enhancements. Hoeller shared personal favorites, design insights, and a glimpse into Spring 5.1, offering developers a roadmap to leverage Spring’s modern capabilities for robust applications.

Who Is Juergen Hoeller?

Juergen Hoeller co-founded the Spring Framework in 2003 and has led its development ever since, overseeing its evolution through GitHub (spring-projects/spring-framework). His deep expertise shaped Spring 5, a major milestone with a Java 8+ baseline. Hoeller’s talk, a design-focused discussion, highlighted how Spring balances annotation-driven and functional paradigms, catering to diverse application needs. His forward-looking perspective connected Spring’s established features to emerging trends like Kotlin and JDK 11.

Spring 5’s New Baseline and Integrations

Spring 5 introduced a Java 8+ baseline, allowing the framework’s internals to use Java 8+ constructs like lambda and Optional, previously optional in Spring 4. This enables new APIs with methods accepting Supplier or CompletableFuture. Hoeller noted Spring 4’s Java 6-based core supported Java 8 applications, but Spring 5 fully embraces Java 8 for both framework and apps. It also integrates modern standards: Servlet 4.0, JPA,2.1, JUnit 5, and Hibernate 5.3, with specific support for Tomcat 9’s push streaming and JPA 8’s Stream. Spring 5 runs on JDK 9, adapting to its deprecations, primarily on the classpath for compatibility with third-party libraries.

Annotation-Based Component Model

Spring’s annotation-based model, refined in Spring 4, remains central. Hoeller showcased a @Controller with @Autowired (optional for single constructors since 4.2), @Transactional, and @Lazy annotations for declarative dependency management. Composable annotations allow custom meta-annotations to combine behaviors, reducing repetition. Configuration classes, introduced in Spring 3, use @Bean for factory methods, with Spring scanning for implicit bean definitions. Spring MVC controllers and endpoints (e.g., @RestController, @GetMapping) follow this model, mapping HTTP requests to handlers with parameter annotations like @PathVariable. This mature, performant approach is Spring’s mainstream in Spring 5.

Functional Programming Paradigm

Spring 5 introduces a functional registration model, challenging annotation reliance. Using GenericApplicationContext, developers can register beans programmatically via registerBean, avoiding reflection or component scanning. Hoeller demonstrated registering a Foo bean with default conventions and a Bar with a lambda-based InstanceSupplier, invoked dynamically. BeanDefinition customizers, also lambdas, add metadata (e.g., lazy initialization) without annotations. Kotlin extensions enhance this, inferring types from lambda returns, making registration concise. A “Gradle-style” Kotlin style uses generics for even terser syntax. This functional style suits reflection-free environments and complements annotation-based approaches, offering flexibility.

Reactive Web Architecture

Spring 5 embraces reactive streams for non-blocking, backpressure-driven interactions. Hoeller contrasted Spring MVC (Servlet-based, blocking, thread pool) with Spring WebFlux (event-loop, non-blocking, using Netty or reactive Servlet engines like Tomcat). WebFlux leverages Project Reactor’s Mono and Flux for reactive endpoints, ideal for high-load or streaming scenarios. Both share MVC-like annotated controllers, but WebFlux’s handlers return reactive publishers, building response pipelines without blocking. Functional endpoints use route functions, mapping requests to handlers programmatically. Hoeller advised using MVC for blocking APIs (e.g., JDBC, JPA) and WebFlux for reactive datastores, noting microservices can mix both.

Hidden Gems in Spring 5

Hoeller highlighted lesser-known features:

  • Nullability Annotations: APIs mark non-null parameters/returns, aiding Java and Kotlin type safety.
  • ObjectProvider Enhancements: New methods like getIfAvailable with Supplier for defaults, improving functional DI.
  • Data Class Binding: Supports Kotlin/Lombok data classes, using constructors for immutable binding without setters.
  • CompletableFuture Scheduling: Enhanced task scheduling with Java 8’s CompletableFuture and java.time APIs.
  • Resource API: Now NIO-based for Java 8.
  • Components Indexer: Build-time indexing speeds up classpath scanning.
  • Logging: Streamlined for SLF4J/Log4j2, no manual bridge setup needed.

These refine Spring’s usability and performance.

Looking Ahead to Spring 5.1

Hoeller previewed Spring 5.1, focusing on JDK 11 support (long-term support release), warning-free module path usage, and potential use of JDK 11’s HTTP client. A “bean stream” API will simplify programmatic bean retrieval, enhancing functional DI. These aim to keep Spring robust for modern Java ecosystems.

Why It Matters

Hoeller’s talk showcases Spring 5’s versatility, blending traditional and cutting-edge paradigms. Functional and reactive programming enable scalable, non-blocking apps, while annotation-driven models ensure familiarity. Hidden gems like nullability and data class support streamline development, and JDK 17 readiness future-proofs Spring. This session inspires developers to explore Spring’s functional APIs, reactive WebFlux, and Kotlin integrations, building applications ready for high-load, distributed environments.

HTTP Cookies Uncovered: A Deep Dive

At Devoxx France 2018, Hubert Sablonnière delivered a talk titled RetourAuxSources Les cookies HTTP, available on YouTube. With a Sherlock-inspired narrative, Sablonnière explored the often-misunderstood world of HTTP cookies, tracing their origins, mechanics, and modern security features like SameSite and cookie prefixes. Through live demos and practical examples, he highlighted their impact on web security, user tracking, and privacy. This session empowers developers to make informed decisions and sparks a broader conversation about the web’s future.

Who Is Hubert Sablonnière?

Hubert Sablonnière, a web developer at Clever Cloud, introduced himself with humor, likening his investigation to Sherlock Holmes. At Clever Cloud, he works on infrastructure automation, enabling developers to focus on coding while the platform handles builds, deployments, and monitoring. His talk aimed to return to the “facts” of HTTP cookies, addressing common misconceptions and their implications for developers and users. Sablonnière’s engaging style and real-world demos made complex concepts accessible, urging attendees to rethink cookies’ role in security and privacy.

The Origins of HTTP Cookies

Sablonnière began with a nod to Lou Montulli, a Netscape engineer who invented HTTP cookies in 1994. Montulli’s contributions to the web are notable: he co-created the Lynx text browser, set up one of the first webcams (FishCam), and introduced the <blink> tag as a playful experiment that became infamous. Cookies were designed to add state to the stateless web, enabling features like e-commerce carts and user sessions across page loads. Sablonnière emphasized Montulli’s lasting impact, as cookies remain a cornerstone of web functionality 24 years later.

What Are HTTP Cookies?

Sablonnière clarified that cookies aren’t just “files stored on a computer,” as often misreported. They’re a protocol where browsers and servers agree to maintain client-side state. When a user visits a site (e.g., cookies.rocks), the server sends a Set-Cookie header with data (e.g., a session ID). The browser stores this in its “cookie jar” and includes it in future requests via the Cookie header. This mechanism, largely unchanged since Netscape’s 1994 spec, supports persistent sessions but raises security and privacy concerns.

Cookie Lifespan and Deletion

Cookies default to session-based storage, expiring when the browser closes, though hibernation can extend this. Servers can set an expiration date (Expires) or duration (Max-Age) in seconds. To delete a cookie, servers set an expiration date in the past (e.g., January 1, 1970). Sablonnière demonstrated this, stressing that understanding these mechanics prevents common errors in session management.

Cookie Scope: Domain and Path

The talk’s core focused on cookie scope, particularly the Domain attribute, which determines when cookies are sent. Without Domain, cookies apply only to the exact hostname (e.g., blue.cookies.rocks). Setting Domain=cookies.rocks extends cookies to subdomains (e.g., blue.cookies.rocks, red.cookies.rocks). Sablonnière’s demo showed how browsers reject cookies for unrelated domains and how the Path attribute restricts cookies to specific URL paths (e.g., /app). A subtle / requirement for Path can trip developers, narrowing cookie scope unexpectedly.

Public Suffix List and Domain Limits

Sablonnière introduced the Public Suffix List (publicsuffix.org), a Mozilla-initiated database of top-level domains (TLDs) and private suffixes (e.g., co.uk, github.io). Browsers use this to prevent cookies from being set for broad TLDs like .com. For example, a cookie for .rocks is invalid, but one for cookies.rocks is allowed. This list, over 12,000 lines, ensures isolation, protecting services like AWS or Clever Cloud from cross-site cookie abuse.

Security Attributes: Secure and HSTS

The Secure attribute ensures cookies are only sent over HTTPS, protecting against interception on public Wi-Fi. Sablonnière warned that HTTP sites could historically set Secure cookies, a flaw addressed in Chrome and Firefox by blocking such cookies from non-HTTPS origins. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) forces browsers to use HTTPS, but he cautioned about its irreversible effects, referencing OWASP guidelines. These measures mitigate risks but require careful implementation.

Cookie Prefixes: Enhancing Trust

Newer standards introduce cookie prefixes: __Secure- and __Host-. __Secure- ensures cookies are set with Secure and sent only over HTTPS. __Host- restricts cookies to the exact hostname (no Domain attribute), Secure, and Path=/, preventing subdomain attacks. Sablonnière noted these are Chrome/Firefox-specific, so servers can’t fully trust them yet, but they signal stronger security guarantees.

Cross-Site Attacks: CSRF and XSS

Cookies enable Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. Sablonnière demonstrated how a malicious site (e.g., foo.example) could trigger a request to cookies.rocks/update_profile with a user’s cookies, altering their profile. The SameSite attribute (Strict or Lax) mitigates this: Strict blocks cookies for cross-site navigation, while Lax allows safe GET requests. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks, where injected scripts access document.cookie, are another threat. The HttpOnly attribute prevents JavaScript access, enhancing security.

Tracking and Privacy Concerns

Sablonnière addressed third-party cookies, used for tracking across sites. Visiting foo.example with an image from cookies.rocks sends cookies.rocks cookies, revealing browsing habits. Blocking third-party cookies (default in Safari) helps, but alternatives like ETags or fingerprinting persist. He highlighted the CNIL’s stance: all trackers, including local storage, require user consent. This raises ethical questions about free content versus privacy, as ads rely on tracking to fund sites.

Alternatives to Cookies

Alternatives like window.name (a 1990s hack) or local storage exist but lack cookies’ automatic request inclusion and expiration controls. Local storage is origin-isolated, unlike cookies, which ignore ports, posing security risks. Sablonnière advocated for OWASP resources to navigate these complexities, urging developers to weigh trade-offs.

Why It Matters

Sablonnière’s talk is a wake-up call to understand cookies’ mechanics and risks. Developers can prevent CSRF/XSS attacks with SameSite and HttpOnly, while users can block third-party cookies. The broader societal question—balancing free content with privacy—remains unresolved. This session inspires developers to secure applications, educate others, and engage in debates about the web’s future.

Reactive Spring: Building Modern Web Apps

At Devoxx France 2018, Juergen Hoeller and Josh Long presented a live-coding session titled Reactive Spring, available on YouTube. As Spring Framework’s co-founder and a Spring developer advocate, they showcased Spring Framework 5’s reactive capabilities, introducing Spring WebFlux, reactive data access, and functional programming. Through a demo-heavy talk, they built a reservation service, blending Java and Kotlin, and explored reactive paradigms across Spring Boot 2, Spring Security 5, and Spring Cloud. This session equips developers to embrace non-blocking, scalable web architectures.

Who Are Juergen Hoeller and Josh Long?

Juergen Hoeller, Spring Framework’s co-founder, leads its development, guiding its evolution since 2003. Josh Long, a Spring developer advocate, brings enthusiasm and practical insights to the community. Their talk, a high-energy live-coding session, flipped the schedule with Hoeller’s earlier Spring 5 talk to accommodate travel. With no slides, they dove into code, demonstrating Spring 5’s reactive stack while humorously highlighting features like Spring Boot’s ASCII banner art. Their expertise and rapport made complex reactive concepts approachable.

Why Reactive Programming?

Hoeller explained reactive programming’s roots in Spring 5, contrasting it with the Servlet-based Spring MVC. Servlets, born from 1990s CGI, assign a thread per HTTP request, blocking until completion—an artificial abstraction over asynchronous network stacks. Reactive streams, inspired by event-driven socket programming, use an event loop with minimal threads (e.g., eight for eight CPU cores). Requests trigger callbacks, avoiding blocking and enabling backpressure, where subscribers control data flow. Spring WebFlux, built on Project Reactor, offers a non-blocking web stack alongside MVC, ideal for high-load scenarios.

Spring WebFlux and Reactive Architecture

Spring WebFlux, introduced in Spring 5, runs on Netty or reactive Servlet containers (e.g., Tomcat), unlike MVC’s thread-per-request model. Hoeller emphasized its event-loop architecture, where HTTP requests are events processed via callbacks. WebFlux supports reactive streams with Reactor’s Mono (0-1 items) and Flux (0-n items), ensuring non-blocking pipelines. Long demonstrated this by initializing a Spring Boot 2 project on start.spring.io, choosing reactive MongoDB and WebFlux, highlighting the absence of reactive JDBC due to its blocking nature.

Live Demo: Building a Reservation Service

Long coded a reservation service managing Reservation entities (ID, name) stored in MongoDB. Using Java 8 (Spring 5’s baseline), he defined a ReservationRepository extending ReactiveCrudRepository, returning Mono or Flux for asynchronous operations. An ApplicationRunner initialized sample data, mapping names to Reservation objects and saving them via flatMap to handle nested publishers. He used Reactor’s operators (thenMany, subscribe) to compose operations, ensuring non-blocking execution. A Kotlin version simplified the entity with data classes, showcasing Spring’s language flexibility.

Annotation-Based vs. Functional Endpoints

The demo included two WebFlux endpoint styles. First, a @RestController with @GetMapping mirrored Spring MVC, returning a Flux<Reservation> from the repository. Hoeller noted that these methods build reactive pipelines, not process requests directly, deferring execution to the runtime. Second, a functional endpoint used RouterFunctions in Kotlin, leveraging a DSL for concise routing (e.g., GET("/reservations")). This programmatic approach, inspired by Java 8 lambdas, avoids annotations and supports complex predicates, offering flexibility for modern apps.

Reactive Ecosystem: Security and Beyond

Hoeller highlighted Spring Security 5’s reactive support, decoupling authentication from Servlet thread-locals to work in WebFlux’s asynchronous context. Long briefly introduced Spring Cloud Gateway, a reactive API gateway for rate limiting and routing, and Spring Cloud Function, a function-as-a-service framework. He deployed a simple Function<Flux<String>, Flux<String>> to Project Riff, a Kubernetes-based runtime, transforming strings to uppercase via Kafka. This showcased reactive programming’s reach into serverless and microservices.

Spring Boot’s Playful Side

Amid technical depth, Long humorously fixated on Spring Boot’s ASCII banner, jokingly criticizing IntelliJ’s “hide banner” option and praising a custom GIF banner (admitting its non-reactive startup delay). This lighthearted digression, complete with audience interaction for demo data names, underscored Spring’s developer-friendly culture while reinforcing the session’s technical focus.

Why It Matters

This talk demystifies reactive programming, showing how Spring 5’s WebFlux, Reactor, and reactive data access enable scalable, non-blocking apps. Developers learn to choose between annotation-based and functional endpoints, integrate with reactive MongoDB, and explore serverless with Riff. The session inspires adopting reactive paradigms for high-throughput systems, leveraging Spring’s robust ecosystem to build future-ready applications.

Back to Basics: HTTP Cookies (2nd version)

HTTP cookies are a ubiquitous part of the web experience, from session management to personalization and, controversially, tracking. Despite their widespread use, their inner workings and historical context are often misunderstood. At Devoxx France 2018, Hubert Sablonnière from Clever Cloud (https://www.clever-cloud.com/) delivered "RetourAuxSources Les cookies HTTP" (Back to Basics: HTTP Cookies). He took the audience on a journey through the origins of cookies, their mechanics, attributes, security implications, and the ongoing debate surrounding privacy and tracking.

Hubert began by transporting the audience back to 1994, introducing Lou Montulli, then at Netscape, who is credited with inventing HTTP cookies. The initial problem was simple: how to maintain state in the inherently stateless HTTP protocol, for things like a virtual shopping cart. This led to the first cookie specification, which has since evolved through several RFCs, with RFC 6265 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265) now being the current standard.

How Cookies Work: The Set-Cookie and Cookie Dance

The fundamental mechanism of cookies involves two HTTP headers. The server sends the Set-Cookie header in an HTTP response to the browser, instructing it to store data for a specific domain and path. Subsequently, the browser sends the Cookie header in requests to the server if the request matches the cookie's criteria.

Hubert meticulously walked through the various attributes that can be set with a cookie, each controlling its behavior. The Expires and Max-Age attributes determine the cookie's lifetime; without them, it becomes a session cookie, deleted when the browser closes. The Domain attribute specifies the domain for which the cookie is valid, potentially including subdomains. Path restricts the cookie to a specific path within the domain. The Secure attribute ensures the cookie is only transmitted over HTTPS. A crucial security attribute, HttpOnly, prevents client-side JavaScript from accessing the cookie, mitigating Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.

SameSite: A Modern Defense Against CSRF

A significant portion of the talk was dedicated to the SameSite attribute, a more recent addition designed to combat Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. CSRF occurs when a malicious website tricks a user's browser into making an unintended request to another site where the user is authenticated. The SameSite attribute, further detailed on MDN Web Docs (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite), controls cookie sending with cross-origin requests and has three values. Strict only sends cookies for same-site requests. Lax, the common default, allows cookies with top-level navigations but not with "unsafe" methods or subresource requests. None allows cookies with all requests but requires the Secure attribute. Hubert emphasized that SameSite=Lax by default is a major step forward in web security.

Cookie Prefixes: Enhancing Integrity

Another modern security feature discussed was cookie prefixes, such as __Secure- and __Host-, with more information available at MDN Web Docs (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Cookies#Cookie_prefixes). If a cookie name starts with __Secure-, the browser requires the Secure attribute. The __Host- prefix is even stronger: it must have the Secure attribute, be set from a secure origin (HTTPS), must not have a Domain attribute (locking it to the host), and must have Path=/. These prefixes help prevent less secure subdomains from overwriting cookies.

Tracking, Privacy, and the Future

The talk delved into the role of cookies in tracking users across the web, a primary driver of privacy concerns. Third-party cookies, set by domains other than the one visited, are the main culprits. Hubert touched upon the web's "grand bargain": free content in exchange for tracking for advertising. He also mentioned browser initiatives like Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention (ITP) and the evolving regulatory landscape like ePrivacy. Hubert concluded by stressing the importance of understanding these web technologies to build more secure and privacy-respecting applications.

Reactive Spring (J. Hoeller, J. Long)

Spring Framework 5 marked a significant evolution, fully embracing reactive programming with Spring WebFlux and Project Reactor. At Devoxx France 2018, Juergen Hoeller, Spring co-founder and Framework lead at VMware, and Josh Long, Spring Developer Advocate at VMware, presented "Reactive Spring". They guided developers through building responsive, resilient, and scalable applications using Spring's reactive features.

Juergen began by explaining the limitations of the traditional servlet model (thread-per-request) under high load or with I/O-bound operations. Reactive programming offers an alternative with an event loop architecture, using few threads to handle many concurrent requests efficiently, especially for asynchronous, non-blocking operations.

Introducing Spring WebFlux and Project Reactor

The cornerstone of reactive programming in Spring is Spring WebFlux, a reactive web framework built for non-blocking I/O. It runs on servers like Netty by default and supports servlet containers with Servlet 3.1+ non-blocking APIs. WebFlux coexists with Spring MVC, offering a choice based on application needs.

Underpinning WebFlux is Project Reactor (https://projectreactor.io/), a fourth-gen reactive library implementing the Reactive Streams specification. Josh introduced Reactor's core types: Mono<T> (0 or 1 element) and Flux<T> (0 to N elements). Both provide operators for transforming, filtering, and combining reactive streams. The Reactive Streams specification ensures interoperability and incorporates backpressure, allowing subscribers to signal their capacity to publishers.

Live Coding: Building Reactive Applications

Josh Long's live coding demonstrated several aspects. Reactive REST Controllers, similar to Spring MVC, use annotations like @RestController but return Mono or Flux. Spring Data has embraced reactive programming (initially project Kay, now modules like Spring Data R2DBC and reactive support for NoSQL databases like MongoDB). The demo showed reactive repositories interacting non-blockingly with databases. WebFlux simplifies streaming data to clients using Server-Sent Events (SSE). As an alternative to annotations, WebFlux offers functional web endpoints with RouterFunction and HandlerFunction. Spring Security 5.0 supports securing reactive applications non-blockingly. The talk also touched on Project Riff (https://projectriff.io/ - now archived), showing how reactive functions could be deployed as FaaS on Kubernetes.

Embracing the Reactive Paradigm

Juergen Hoeller and Josh Long emphasized that reactive programming is a different way of thinking about application architecture and data flow, encouraging systems that are responsive, resilient, and resource-efficient. Spring Framework 5 provides a comprehensive platform for adopting this paradigm.

Asynchronous Decision-Making: Why and How? (B. Delacrétaz)

In distributed teams and open-source projects, synchronous meetings are often impractical. At Devoxx France 2018, Bertrand Delacrétaz, Principal Scientist at Adobe and Apache Software Foundation (ASF) contributor, presented "Prise de décisions asynchrone, pourquoi et comment?" He shared how asynchronous techniques from communities like Apache foster effective collaboration, better documentation, and inclusive outcomes.

Bertrand highlighted challenges of global teams: time zones, cultural differences, and meeting costs. He noted that open-source projects, particularly the ASF, demonstrate that decision-making without constant meetings is preferable.

Core Principles of Asynchronous Decision-Making

Bertrand Delacrétaz outlined key principles from ASF practices. Everything in Writing (The Written Trace) is crucial: all significant discussions, proposals, and decisions must be documented, typically on mailing lists or issue trackers. The Apache mantra "If it's not on the mailing list, it didn't happen" underscores this. Lazy Consensus states that if a proposal faces no objections within a reasonable timeframe (e.g., 72 hours), it's accepted; silence implies consent. For formal decisions, the ASF uses a "+1, 0, -1" voting system. A +1 means agreement and willingness to help. A -1 (veto) requires technical justification and a counter-proposal, focusing disagreements on merit. Defined Roles, like facilitator or moderator, guide discussions and ensure process continuity.

Tools for Asynchronous Collaboration

The process uses simple tools: Mailing Lists for discussions and decisions ; Issue Trackers (Jira, GitHub Issues) for tasks and related discussions ; Wikis for stable documentation and decision summaries ; and Voting/Polling Tools.

Benefits and Making Meetings Better

Bertrand argued for significant benefits from asynchronous decision-making. It promotes Inclusivity by allowing participation across time zones and schedules. It leads to Better Considered Decisions as participants have time to reflect and research. It Reduces "Meeting Culture" by freeing time from inefficient meetings. It creates a Valuable Archive of discussions and decision rationale. This doesn't eliminate meetings but reserves them for complex discussions truly needing real-time interaction, prepared with asynchronous documentation. Bertrand encouraged teams to adopt these practices for improved efficiency, transparency, and collaboration.

Spark Optimization and Performance (I. Beauvais, B. Bouchahoua)

Apache Spark is a cornerstone in big data, known for speed and versatility, but optimal performance can be elusive. At Devoxx France 2018, Ivan Beauvais and Bruno Bouchahoua from Exaltan (https://www.exaltan.fr/) presented "Optimisation et performance sur Spark". They shared practical advice for Spark 2.x on YARN with HDFS, focusing on diagnosing and addressing common performance issues.

The presentation highlighted Spark's multifaceted nature—supporting multiple languages, cluster managers (YARN, Kubernetes), and use cases (SQL, Streaming, ML). This complexity means various user profiles interact with Spark differently, often leading to performance challenges.

Understanding Spark's Core: RDDs, Dependencies, and Shuffles

The talk revisited Spark's Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs). Key concepts include Initial Partitioning, where the number of input HDFS files often determines initial RDD partitions. Spark operations are transformations (creating new RDDs) or actions (triggering computation). Narrow dependencies allow pipelined execution on a single partition, while wide dependencies (e.g., groupByKey, reduceByKey, joins) require data shuffling across partitions, creating new stages. reduceByKey is generally preferred over groupByKey as it performs pre-aggregation on the map side, reducing shuffle data. The speakers illustrated how groupByKey shuffles all values for a key to a single reducer, while reduceByKey optimizes this by reducing locally first.

DataFrames, Datasets, and the Catalyst Optimizer

Spark 2.x heavily promotes the DataFrame and Dataset APIs, which benefit from the Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine. Catalyst builds an optimized execution plan, performing logical and physical optimizations, while Tungsten provides efficient code generation and off-heap memory management. Using these APIs often yields better performance than raw RDDs due to these internal optimizations. The explain() method is vital for understanding the query plans generated by Catalyst.

Partitioning, Skew, and Serialization

Effective partitioning is critical. Operations like repartition() (full shuffle, can increase/decrease partitions) and coalesce() (minimizes shuffles, only decreases partitions) help manage data distribution. Data skew, where some partitions are much larger than others, can cripple performance; techniques like salting keys can mitigate this. For serialization, Kryo (https://github.com/EsotericSoftware/kryo) is recommended over Java's default for custom objects in RDDs, as it's faster and more compact. DataFrames/Datasets handle serialization more efficiently internally.

Memory Management, Joins, and Caching

Understanding Spark's memory management (on-heap vs. off-heap with Tungsten) is key. The Spark UI is indispensable for monitoring memory usage, GC pressure, and task execution. Regarding joins, Spark chooses strategies like Broadcast Hash Join (for small table joins, use broadcast() hint), Shuffle Hash Join, or Sort Merge Join. Analyzing the Spark UI helps identify join strategies and potential bottlenecks. Caching (.cache() or .persist()) RDDs/DataFrames can save recomputation but must be used judiciously, considering memory impact and storage levels (memory-only, disk, etc.).

Monitor Kafka Like a Pro (G. Shapira, X. Léauté)

Apache Kafka is a central nervous system for data flow in many businesses, making its robust monitoring an operational necessity, not a luxury. At Devoxx France 2018, Gwen Shapira, then with Confluent and now with a stealth startup, and Xavier Léauté, Staff Software Engineer at Confluent (https://www.confluent.io/), shared their expertise in "Monitor Kafka Like a Pro". They presented best practices through real-world scenarios, covering broker issues, client-side problems, and replication monitoring.

Xavier Léauté started by noting that while users often feel overwhelmed by Kafka metrics, the reality is often a lack of any monitoring setup, leading to zero visibility during issues.

Scenario 1: Broker Issues After an Upgrade

Gwen Shapira tackled the common scenario: "We upgraded Kafka, started it, and now something is really wrong with a broker." The first step is data collection: logs and metrics. Log Analysis: Look for stack dumps around the error timeframe. An OutOfMemoryError is a clear indicator of problems. Garbage Collection (GC) Logs: Tools like GCEasy.io (https://gceasy.io/) can analyze GC logs. Long GC pauses can cause ZooKeeper session timeouts (Kafka 0.10.1.0 increased the default from 3s to 6s, configurable zookeeper.session.timeout.ms). If GC pauses are too long, brokers get kicked out of the cluster. Key metrics to check include heap usage (bytes after GC) and GC throughput (percentage of time not spent in GC – aim for >90-95%). Broker Metrics: Essential metrics include:

* `kafka.server:type=KafkaRequestHandlerPool,name=RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent`: Should be above 30%; if near zero, the broker is overloaded. 
* `kafka.network:type=RequestMetrics,name=TotalTimeMs`: Provides request latency (produce, fetch) percentiles. High latency indicates issues. 
* `kafka.server:type=BrokerTopicMetrics,name=MessagesInPerSec`: Message ingress rate. 
* `kafka.log:type=Log,name=LogEndOffset`: Size of logs. 
* Under-replicated partitions (`kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions`): Should be zero. Non-zero indicates data loss risk or unavailability if `min.insync.replicas` isn't met. 
* ISR (In-Sync Replica) shrink/expand rate (`kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=IsrShrinksPerSec`, `IsrExpandsPerSec`): High rates signal unstable ISR sets.

OS Metrics: CPU utilization, memory, disk I/O (especially iowait), and network traffic are critical. Disk issues are common; Kafka is I/O intensive.

Scenario 2: Troublesome Kafka Application (Client-Side)

Xavier Léauté then discussed diagnosing a misbehaving Kafka application. Consumer Lag: This is the most critical client-side metric (kafka.consumer:type=consumer-fetch-manager-metrics,client-id="{client_id}",topic="{topic}",partition="{partition}",name=records-lag). It shows how far behind a consumer is from the end of the log. High lag means the consumer isn't keeping up. Analyzing consumer group assignments can reveal imbalances (e.g., one consumer instance handling more partitions than others). Tools like Burrow (from LinkedIn, now open source) help monitor consumer lag across multiple clusters. Producer Metrics:

* `kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics,client-id="{client_id}",name=record-error-rate`: Should be zero. 
* `kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics,client-id="{client_id}",name=request-latency-avg`: Average time for produce requests. 
* `kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics,client-id="{client_id}",name=batch-size-avg`: Average batch size. Tune `batch.size` and `linger.ms` for throughput. 
* `kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics,client-id="{client_id}",name=compression-rate-avg`: Monitor effectiveness of compression.

Consumer Metrics:

* `kafka.consumer:type=consumer-metrics,client-id="{client_id}",name=commit-latency-avg`: Time taken to commit offsets. 
* `kafka.consumer:type=consumer-fetch-manager-metrics,client-id="{client_id}",name=records-per-request-avg`: How many records are fetched per request. 
* `max.poll.interval.ms`: If processing takes too long, the consumer might be kicked out of the group. Profile application processing time. Consider if data skew is causing uneven processing loads.

Scenario 3: End-to-End Monitoring and Replication

Gwen Shapira returned to discuss monitoring the entire pipeline. End-to-End Latency: Critical for understanding user experience. Deploy "canary" or "synthetic" producers/consumers that send a test message and measure the time until it's received. This helps isolate if latency issues are Kafka-side, network-side, or application-side. Replication: min.insync.replicas (ISR) is a key configuration for durability. If the number of ISRs drops below this, producers with acks=all will fail. Monitor UnderReplicatedPartitions and ISR shrink/expand rates. Gwen emphasized that problems often span multiple components. For instance, a slow consumer might cause producer backpressure if buffers fill up, even if the brokers are healthy. Monitoring logs and metrics across brokers, producers, consumers, ZooKeeper, OS, and network is essential for a holistic view.

The speakers concluded by highlighting Confluent's resources, including their blog, demos for monitoring tools, and a large Slack community for Kafka users.

Modern Android Development (R. Guy, C. Haase)

The Android development landscape has evolved significantly since its inception, with new tools, APIs, and best practices emerging. At Devoxx France 2018, Romain Guy and Chet Haase, both from Google's Android team, presented "Modern Android Development". They contrasted old and new approaches across various aspects of app development, aiming to guide developers on what they should know and use.

Chet Haase began by noting that much old advice, while relevant a decade ago, is now outdated due to platform advancements. The talk's goal was to update this advice for the modern era.

Tools: From Hierarchy Viewer to Layout Inspector

Old Way: Hierarchy Viewer was a standalone tool for debugging view hierarchies. While useful, it could be cumbersome. New Way: The Layout Inspector, integrated within Android Studio, offers a more powerful and user-friendly way to inspect and debug layouts in real-time. It provides detailed attributes for each view and a 3D visualization of the layout hierarchy, making it easier to spot overlapping views or deep nesting.

Layouts: Embracing ConstraintLayout

Old Way: Developers often relied on nested LinearLayout and RelativeLayout instances, which could lead to deep view hierarchies that were inefficient and caused performance problems during measure and layout passes. New Way: ConstraintLayout is now the recommended way to build complex and responsive UIs. It allows for flat view hierarchies by defining relationships (constraints) between widgets, similar to RelativeLayout but more powerful and flexible. The visual editor for ConstraintLayout within Android Studio is also a significant advantage, enabling developers to design layouts graphically.

Background Processing: Coroutines and WorkManager

Old Way: AsyncTask was commonly used for simple background tasks. However, it suffered from issues like memory leaks related to Activity lifecycles and could become unwieldy for complex operations. New Way: For asynchronous operations tied to a UI component's lifecycle, Kotlin Coroutines are highly recommended. They provide a cleaner, more concise way to write asynchronous code and integrate well with lifecycles. For deferrable and guaranteed background work (even if the app exits), WorkManager is the preferred solution. It handles constraints like network availability or charging status and ensures tasks run reliably.

Permissions: Runtime Requests

Old Way: Permissions were requested at install time. Users had to accept all permissions upfront, or not install the app. New Way: Since Android 6.0 (API 23), apps must request runtime permissions for dangerous permissions. This means asking the user for specific permissions only when the app actually needs to perform an operation requiring that permission, providing better context and control to the user.

Language: The Rise of Kotlin

Old Way: Java was the primary language for Android development. New Way: Kotlin is now an officially supported language for Android development and is increasingly preferred. It offers null safety, conciseness, interoperability with Java, and features like extension functions that can make Android APIs more pleasant to use (e.g., via Android KTX libraries). Data classes in Kotlin significantly reduce boilerplate for model objects.

Architecture: Embracing Architecture Components

Old Way: Android lacked a strong, opinionated architecture, often leading to Activity or Fragment classes becoming bloated ("God objects"), tightly coupled, and difficult to test. Managing UI state across configuration changes (like screen rotation) was also a common pain point. New Way: Android Architecture Components (ViewModel, LiveData, Room, Lifecycle-aware components) provide a set of libraries to build robust, testable, and maintainable apps.

* **ViewModel**: Stores and manages UI-related data in a lifecycle-conscious way, surviving configuration changes. 
* **LiveData**: An observable data holder that is lifecycle-aware, meaning it only updates UI components that are in an active lifecycle state. 
* **Room**: An abstraction layer over SQLite that provides compile-time query verification and reduces boilerplate.

Lists: RecyclerView and Paging Library

Old Way: ListView was the go-to for displaying scrollable lists of items. While functional, it was less efficient than its successor and required more boilerplate (e.g., the ViewHolder pattern had to be manually implemented for performance). New Way: RecyclerView is a more flexible and efficient way to display large datasets. It enforces the ViewHolder pattern, promotes UI component reuse, and enables various layout managers (LinearLayoutManager, GridLayoutManager, StaggeredGridLayoutManager). For handling very large or infinitely scrolling lists, the Paging Library (part of Architecture Components) helps load data in chunks, reducing memory usage and improving performance.

Romain Guy and Chet Haase concluded by reiterating that while old methods still work, adopting these modern approaches leads to better, more robust, and more maintainable Android applications.

So Why Are We Still Coding in JavaScript? (W. Goedel)

The world of frontend development is awash with languages that compile to JavaScript, such as TypeScript, ReasonML, PureScript, and Elm, all promising to make developers' lives easier. At Devoxx France 2018, Wolfram Goedel, a developer with twenty years of experience in JavaScript and explorations into TypeScript, Elm, and ReasonML, posed the question: "Mais alors pourquoi encore coder en JavaScript ?" (So why are we still coding in JavaScript?). His talk was not a dismissal of JavaScript, which he described as an elegant, if somewhat dangerously flexible language, but rather a reflection on the costs and benefits of adopting typed systems and functional paradigms when targeting JavaScript runtimes.

Wolfram began by acknowledging the allure of these newer languages. They often introduce strong typing, which can catch many common errors at compile time rather than runtime, leading to more robust applications. Functional programming concepts, prevalent in languages like Elm and PureScript, promise benefits like immutability, pure functions, and easier state management, which can simplify complex UIs and reduce side effects. Wolfram shared his experiences, noting that languages like TypeScript offer a gradual path to typing an existing JavaScript codebase, while Elm provides a more opinionated, purely functional approach that can be very productive once its learning curve is surmounted. ReasonML, with its OCaml roots and Facebook backing, aims to bring powerful type inference and functional features with a syntax that feels more familiar to JavaScript developers.

The JavaScript Ecosystem and Developer Experience

Despite the advantages of these compile-to-JS languages, JavaScript itself continues to dominate. Wolfram explored several reasons for this. Firstly, the JavaScript ecosystem is vast and mature. The sheer number of libraries, frameworks (like React, Angular, Vue), and tools available for JavaScript is unparalleled. While many compile-to-JS languages can interoperate with JavaScript, the integration is not always seamless, and a direct JavaScript approach often offers a smoother developer experience in terms of tooling and community support.

Secondly, JavaScript has evolved significantly. Features introduced in ECMAScript 2015 (ES6) and subsequent versions, such as classes, modules, arrow functions, promises, and async/await, have addressed many of the language's earlier pain points and made it more expressive and capable of handling large-scale applications. This evolution reduces some of the immediate pressure to switch to an alternative language for features that are now becoming native to JavaScript.

The Cost of Abstraction and Tooling

Wolfram also touched upon the "cost of abstraction." While compile-to-JS languages provide benefits, they also introduce an additional layer of tooling and complexity. Developers need to manage build processes, source maps for debugging, and understand how the abstractions translate to JavaScript. This can sometimes lead to a steeper learning curve and a more opaque development process, especially when issues arise that require delving into the generated JavaScript. The perceived productivity gains from a typed or functional language must be weighed against the cognitive overhead and potential friction introduced by the toolchain.

Furthermore, Wolfram argued that the dynamic nature of JavaScript, often cited as a weakness, can also be a strength, allowing for rapid prototyping and flexibility that some developers find productive. He emphasized that good development practices, testing, and a disciplined approach can mitigate many of the risks associated with JavaScript's dynamism.

A Call for a Shared Vocabulary

Ultimately, Wolfram Goedel suggested that the question isn't about an outright replacement of JavaScript but about understanding the trade-offs and choosing the right tools for the job and the team. He advocated for developers to become familiar with the concepts offered by typed systems and functional programming, even if they continue to primarily write JavaScript. This shared vocabulary and understanding of different paradigms enrich the developer community and can lead to better software design, regardless of the specific language used. The "why" of still coding in JavaScript, for many, comes down to its massive ecosystem, its ongoing evolution, and a developer experience that, for all its quirks, remains highly productive and accessible.
