LinuxKit: The IKEA-Style Linux (PY. Aillet, E. Briand)

For years, building a Linux distribution "from scratch" has been a complex and often perilous undertaking, typically reserved for the most dedicated enthusiasts. However, LinuxKit, a project initiated by Docker Inc., offers a modern, tool-driven approach to crafting custom Linux operating systems, making the process almost as straightforward as assembling IKEA furniture (though a manual is still helpful!). At Devoxx France 2018, Pierre-Yves Aillet and Eric Briand, both from Zenika, presented "Linuxkit le linux façon ikea," delving into the project's genesis, concepts, and ecosystem, and demonstrating how to build a custom distribution live.

The core idea behind LinuxKit is to create minimalist, secure, and maintainable operating systems specifically designed for running containers. Pierre-Yves and Eric began by highlighting the difference between traditional Virtual Machines (VMs) and containers. VMs package an application with its libraries and an entire guest OS, leading to larger footprints and slower boot times. Containers, on the other hand, share the host OS kernel and package only the application and its dependencies, resulting in lighter, faster deployments. LinuxKit aims to provide the ideal host OS for these containers—nothing more, nothing less.

Genesis and Core Concepts

LinuxKit emerged from Docker's own needs. For products like Docker for Mac and Docker for Windows, a lightweight Linux VM is required to run Docker containers on non-Linux hosts. Docker needed a way to build these VMs that was secure, minimal, and easily reproducible. Traditional distributions were often too bloated or didn't offer the desired level of customization and security focus.

The key concepts underpinning LinuxKit include immutability, a component-based architecture, and security by default. LinuxKit systems are designed to be immutable; they are built once and are not typically modified in place. Updates involve replacing the entire OS image. The OS itself is composed of a collection of containerized components (services, kernel, filesystem tools) defined in a YAML file. This declarative approach makes the system predictable and easy to version control. Security is a primary concern, with features like read-only root filesystems by default and a minimal attack surface.

Building with Moby and LinuxKit

The speakers introduced the Moby project, an open framework created by Docker to assemble specialized container systems. LinuxKit is a key component of the Moby project, providing the tooling to build the actual OS images. Building a LinuxKit OS involves a YAML file that describes the desired components:

  • Kernel: Specifies the Linux kernel image and command-line arguments.
  • Init: Defines the init process, which is itself a container. LinuxKit often uses containerd as an init process.
  • Onboot: A list of containers to run once during system startup, typically for setup tasks.
  • Services: Long-running system services, also packaged as containers (e.g., containerd, sshd, logging services).
  • Files: Allows inclusion of arbitrary files into the OS image.
  • Trust: Defines how image trust and signing are handled, integrating with Notary for secure image distribution.

The build process, managed by the moby tool, takes this YAML definition, fetches the specified container images (often from Docker Hub), and assembles them into a bootable OS image in various formats (ISO, raw disk, AMI for AWS, VHD for Azure, etc.).

Live Demonstrations and Use Cases

Pierre-Yves Aillet and Eric Briand conducted live demos, showcasing how quickly a custom LinuxKit OS could be defined and built. They demonstrated building a minimal image that simply booted and ran a few services, then moved on to more complex examples, such as an image capable of running Docker containers itself or even a Kubernetes node. This highlighted the flexibility of LinuxKit in tailoring an OS to specific needs.

Use cases for LinuxKit are diverse. Beyond Docker for Mac/Windows, it's suitable for embedded systems, specialized appliances, and creating secure, minimal host environments for container orchestrators like Kubernetes or Docker Swarm. Companies like HPE and Microsoft are also involved in the project, contributing and using LinuxKit for their own purposes. The project's focus on security and minimalism makes it an attractive option for environments where a small footprint and reduced attack surface are critical.

How the Decentralized Web Works (A. Cailly)

Concerns are growing about the control that certain companies and governments have over our internet usage. In response, many advocate for web decentralization, similar to how Mastodon offers an alternative to Twitter. However, the concepts required for this shift are quite different from the traditional client-server applications that dominate today. At Devoxx France 2018, Antoine Cailly from Zenika presented "Le web décentralisé, comment ça marche ?" (The decentralized web, how does it work?). He aimed to explain simply, with examples, what is needed to decentralize the web, delving into some technical mechanisms like DHTs, Merkle trees, and CRDTs, and highlighting initiatives that could reshape our future usage.

Antoine began by illustrating the problems of the centralized web, such as censorship and data suppression. For instance, Wikipedia has been blocked in Turkey, and an alternative snapshot was made available on the peer-to-peer network IPFS (InterPlanetary File System). Similarly, data related to climate change, removed from US government sites, found refuge on peer-to-peer networks like BitTorrent through initiatives such as the DataRefuge project. These examples underscore the need for systems where data is not controlled by a single entity.

Core Concepts of Decentralization

Antoine Cailly then moved on to the technical underpinnings of decentralization. A key challenge is data addressing. In the current web, data is location-addressed (e.g., by URL, which points to a server). Decentralized systems often use content-addressing, where data is identified by a hash of its content. This means that if you have the hash, you can retrieve the data from any peer who has it, without needing to know a specific server location. This is fundamental to systems like IPFS and BitTorrent.

To find peers who have the desired content, decentralized networks often use Distributed Hash Tables (DHTs). A DHT is a distributed system that provides a lookup service similar to a hash table; given a key (e.g., a content hash), it returns associated values (e.g., the IP addresses of peers storing that content). Kademlia is a popular DHT algorithm used by BitTorrent and IPFS.

Ensuring data integrity is another crucial aspect. Merkle trees (or hash trees) play a vital role here. In a Merkle tree, a large piece of data is broken into chunks, each chunk is hashed, then pairs of hashes are hashed together, and so on, until a single root hash is obtained. This root hash uniquely identifies the entire dataset. If any part of the data is altered, the root hash will change, making tampering evident. This allows peers to verify the integrity of data received from untrusted sources.

Handling Dynamic Data and Identity

While content-addressing and Merkle trees are excellent for static data, dynamic data presents more challenges. This is where Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) come into play. CRDTs are data structures designed to be replicated across multiple computers in a network, where updates can be made concurrently without coordination, and are guaranteed to eventually converge to the same state. This is essential for building collaborative applications or social networks on decentralized platforms.

Identity management is also a significant hurdle. In a decentralized web, how do you prove you are who you say you are without a central authority? Systems like PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) have long offered solutions using public-key cryptography. Newer initiatives like IPNS (InterPlanetary Naming System) in IPFS allow users to associate a mutable pointer (linked to a cryptographic key pair) to content hashes, enabling updatable content linked to a persistent identity. Secure Scuttlebutt (SSB) is another decentralized protocol that uses cryptographic identities and an append-only log model for social networking.

Promising Initiatives

Antoine highlighted several projects pushing the boundaries of the decentralized web:

  • IPFS (InterPlanetary File System): A peer-to-peer hypermedia protocol designed to make the web faster, safer, and more open.
  • Dat Project: A peer-to-peer data sharing tool focused on versioning and syncing datasets.
  • Secure Scuttlebutt (SSB): A decentralized social network protocol based on an append-only log design, often used for off-grid communication.
  • Mastodon: A federated microblogging platform, often seen as a decentralized alternative to Twitter, though it relies on federated servers rather than being purely peer-to-peer for all interactions.

Antoine Cailly concluded by emphasizing that while the decentralized web is still evolving and faces many challenges, its underlying technologies offer powerful solutions for building a more resilient, open, and user-controlled internet.

Is Today's Code Freed from the von Neumann Imperative Style? (T. Jaskula)

Forty years have passed since John Backus delivered his 1977 Turing Award lecture, "Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style? A Functional Style and Its Algebra of Programs." This visionary paper identified a fundamental problem in programming thought, critiquing the imperative programming paradigm dominated by the von Neumann style since the 1950s. Despite the rising popularity of functional programming, enterprise development today is largely dominated by object-oriented languages like Java and C#. At Devoxx France 2018, Tomasz Jaskula, from his company OCTO Technology and involved with Neo4j Kraph Mappers and the Paris #ddde/#rest & #fsharp meetups, revisited this question: "Le code d'aujourd'hui est il libéré du style impératif à la von Neumann ?" (Is today's code freed from the von Neumann imperative style?). He explored whether Backus's critique remains valid by inspecting code examples from both object-oriented and functional languages, demonstrating that even when using OO languages, developers often remain entrenched in von Neumann-style imperative thinking.

Tomasz began by setting the stage, acknowledging Backus's profound impact and the core of his argument: the von Neumann style of programming, characterized by step-by-step instruction execution, mutable state, and assignment statements, creates a "bottleneck" both conceptually and in terms of program reasoning. Backus advocated for a functional style that emphasizes expressions, immutability, and higher-order functions, which he believed could lead to more robust, verifiable, and parallelizable programs.

The Persistence of Imperative Thinking

Tomasz Jaskula argued that despite the availability of functional features in modern OO languages (like lambdas and streams in Java), the dominant mindset often remains imperative. He presented code snippets, contrasting typical imperative solutions with their functional counterparts. For example, a common loop for iterating and transforming a collection in Java using an external iterator and mutable accumulators was compared to a more declarative approach using the Stream API, map, and collect. While the latter uses functional constructs, Tomasz pointed out that the underlying thinking can still be driven by an imperative sequence of operations if developers don't fully embrace the paradigm shift.

He highlighted how object-oriented programming, while offering benefits like encapsulation and polymorphism, doesn't inherently free developers from the von Neumann style if objects are primarily seen as bags of mutable state that are procedurally manipulated. The focus often remains on how to perform computations (the sequence of steps) rather than what computation to perform (the declarative expression of intent). This can lead to code that is harder to reason about, more prone to side effects, and less amenable to concurrency.

The "Word-at-a-Time" Bottleneck

A key aspect of Backus's critique was the "word-at-a-time" nature of von Neumann programming, where programs operate on individual data elements sequentially. Functional programming, with its emphasis on operations over entire data structures (e.g., mapping a function over a list), aims to break this bottleneck. Tomasz showed how this difference manifests in code, leading to more concise and potentially more efficient solutions when the functional approach is truly adopted.

He also touched upon the "assignment problem"—the pervasive use of assignment to mutable variables, which Backus saw as a major source of complexity. Immutability, a cornerstone of many functional languages and increasingly adopted in OO contexts, helps to alleviate this by ensuring that data, once created, does not change, simplifying state management and reasoning about program behavior over time.

Are We Liberated?

Tomasz Jaskula's conclusion was nuanced. While modern languages provide tools that can liberate programmers from the strict von Neumann style, the liberation is not automatic. It requires a conscious shift in thinking, moving from an imperative, state-centric view to a more declarative, expression-oriented one. The danger, he suggested, is that developers might use functional-looking syntax without truly escaping the underlying imperative thought patterns learned and reinforced over decades.

He urged the audience to reflect on their own coding practices and to explore different paradigms not just syntactically but conceptually. The biggest problem, he posited, is being confined by established thought patterns without realizing that other paradigms exist, or worse, forgetting that alternative ways of thinking about programming have been around for a long time. True liberation, in the Backusian sense, requires an ongoing effort to learn, question, and evolve our mental models of computation.

IoT Security: Difficulties, Flaws, and Countermeasures (A. Duque)

The proliferation of connected objects in our daily lives has made the security of these electronic devices, often overlooked in the past, a real issue. Their low design cost, manufacturer negligence, and even our own oversight as developers make them easy targets for hackers. This phenomenon is evident in the news, with increasing reports of large-scale attacks targeting connected cameras, refrigerators, and even Bluetooth locks. At Devoxx France 2018, Alexis Duque, a research engineer at Rtone and a doctoral student at the CITI laboratory (INSA Lyon), presented "La sécurité dans l'IoT difficultés, failles et contre mesures" (IoT Security: Difficulties, Flaws, and Countermeasures). His talk detailed recent attacks, common IoT vulnerabilities (referencing the OWASP IoT Top 10), and explored solutions, with a focus on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and side-channel attacks.

Alexis began by defining the Internet of Things (IoT), noting Gartner's prediction of 20 billion connected objects by 2020. IoT encompasses not just devices connected to the internet, but any object that connects to a phone or another object and includes some level of intelligence. He then introduced the three pillars of security: Confidentiality (preventing unauthorized disclosure of information), Integrity (ensuring data is not altered improperly), and Availability (making sure systems are accessible when needed).

Common IoT Vulnerabilities and OWASP IoT Top 10

A significant portion of the presentation focused on common vulnerabilities found in IoT devices, many of which are highlighted in the OWASP IoT Project's Top 10. Alexis Duque discussed several of these:

  1. Weak, Guessable, or Hardcoded Passwords: A very common issue where devices ship with default credentials that are well-known or easily guessed (e.g., "admin/admin"). He cited the Mirai botnet, which exploited this to create a massive DDoS attack.
  2. Insecure Network Services: IoT devices often run unnecessary network services (e.g., Telnet, FTP) that can be exploited if not properly secured. Shodan is a search engine that can find such exposed devices.
  3. Insecure Ecosystem Interfaces: This includes insecure web interfaces, mobile applications, or cloud backends used to manage or interact with IoT devices. Common web vulnerabilities like XSS or SQL injection can affect the entire IoT ecosystem.
  4. Lack of Secure Update Mechanism: Many IoT devices lack a secure way to receive firmware updates, or the update process itself is vulnerable, allowing attackers to flash malicious firmware. Using signed firmware is crucial.
  5. Use of Insecure or Outdated Components: Devices may use libraries or software components with known vulnerabilities. The Heartbleed bug in OpenSSL was a prime example affecting many systems, including IoT.
  6. Insufficient Privacy Protection: IoT devices often collect sensitive personal data without adequate protection or user consent.
  7. Insecure Data Transfer and Storage: Data transmitted or stored by IoT devices (e.g., on the device, in the cloud, or via mobile app) is often not encrypted or is encrypted using weak methods.

Alexis emphasized the importance of threat modeling during the design phase to anticipate potential attacks.

Focus on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) Security

Given its prevalence in IoT, Alexis dedicated a segment to Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) security. He explained the pairing process in BLE, including different association models like Just Works (no authentication), Passkey Entry, and Out-Of-Band. While BLE has evolved with security features like LE Secure Connections, vulnerabilities still exist. He demonstrated a Man-in-the-Middle (MiTM) attack using tools like gatttool and a Raspberry Pi to intercept and manipulate BLE communication, highlighting how an attacker could potentially unlock a Bluetooth-enabled door lock. He also mentioned the BlueBorne attack, a set of airborne vulnerabilities affecting Bluetooth.

Side-Channel Attacks

A more advanced topic covered was side-channel attacks. These attacks don't exploit weaknesses in the algorithm's code (like buffer overflows) but rather information gained from the physical implementation of a cryptosystem. Examples include:

  • Timing Attacks: Analyzing the time taken to perform cryptographic operations.
  • Power Monitoring Attacks: Observing the power consumption of a device during computation. Simple Power Analysis (SPA) and Differential Power Analysis (DPA) can reveal secret keys.
  • Electromagnetic Attacks: Detecting electromagnetic emanations.

Countermeasures include adding noise, randomizing computations, or using specific hardware shields.

Solutions and Future Directions

Alexis Duque concluded by discussing solutions. For developers, this includes following secure coding practices, using strong authentication, encrypting data, implementing secure update mechanisms, and minimizing the attack surface by disabling unnecessary services. He mentioned the importance of penetration testing and security audits. Emerging solutions include hardware security elements like Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) or secure enclaves, and exploring newer, more secure communication protocols. He also pointed to ongoing research in areas like lightweight cryptography suitable for resource-constrained IoT devices.

JHipster: What's New in Our Spring/Summer 2018 Collection (J. Dubois, D. K Sasidharan)

JHipster, the popular application generator, boasts over 400 contributors and evolves rapidly, making it challenging to keep up with its new features. At Devoxx France 2018, Julien Dubois, creator of JHipster and working at Ippon Technologies, and Deepu K Sasidharan, co-lead of JHipster working at GigaSpaces, detailed the noteworthy additions in JHipster 5, their latest release at the time. The presentation covered Spring Boot 2, enhanced React and Angular support, code refactoring, security improvements, caching, and scalability.

Julien and Deepu started with a brief introduction to JHipster for newcomers. JHipster is an application generator focusing on developer productivity, initially combining Spring Boot on the backend with Angular on the frontend. It has since expanded to include React as a frontend option and generates comprehensive development and production workflows. A key strength of JHipster is its large and active community.

Key Features in JHipster 5

JHipster 5 brought several significant updates. A major highlight was the upgrade to Spring Boot 2.0. This involved migrating to the latest versions of Spring Framework, Spring Security, and other Spring ecosystem projects, bringing performance improvements and new features from the Spring world, including reactive capabilities with WebFlux (though JHipster's core remained servlet-based at this point, reactive options were being explored).

On the frontend, React support became official and a first-class citizen alongside Angular. The JHipster team had invested heavily in making the React experience as polished as the Angular one, using Create React App as a base and integrating popular libraries like Redux for state management. For Angular users, JHipster 5 continued to support the latest Angular versions, improving the generated code structure and leveraging the Angular CLI more effectively.

Code refactoring and quality were also focal points. The generated codebase saw improvements in organization and clarity. JHipster 5 embraced Prettier for code formatting, ensuring consistent code style across generated projects and among development teams. This automated formatting helps reduce bikeshedding on code style during reviews.

Enhancements in Security, Caching, and Scalability

Security is always a critical concern, and JHipster 5 continued to enhance its security posture. This included updates to Spring Security integration, improved JWT (JSON Web Token) handling, and options for OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect integration with identity providers like Keycloak or Okta. The team emphasized keeping dependencies up-to-date to mitigate known vulnerabilities.

For caching, JHipster has long supported various caching providers like Ehcache, Hazelcast, and Infinispan. JHipster 5 refined these integrations, particularly with Spring Boot 2's caching abstractions, making it easier to configure and use caching effectively to improve performance.

Scalability considerations were addressed through improved support for microservices architectures. JHipster provides robust tooling for generating microservices and gateways, integrating with technologies like Netflix Eureka for service discovery, Spring Cloud Config for centralized configuration, and monitoring tools like the ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or Prometheus. Docker and Kubernetes deployment options were also further streamlined.

Roadmap and Future Directions

Julien Dubois and Deepu K Sasidharan concluded with a look at the JHipster roadmap. Plans included further embracing reactive programming with Spring WebFlux, exploring alternative frontend frameworks like Vue.js, enhancing support for serverless architectures, and continuing to improve the developer experience and generated code quality. The strong community involvement remained a cornerstone for driving JHipster's evolution. They also promoted the JHipster Conf, a dedicated conference for the JHipster community.

JDK 9 Mission Accomplished: What Next For Java? (S. Ritter)

The release of JDK 9 in September 2017 brought many changes to the Java platform, the most significant being the Java Platform Module System (JPMS), often referred to as Project Jigsaw. This monumental effort broke up the monolithic rt.jar into 97 modules and, importantly, encapsulated internal APIs like sun.misc.Unsafe that developers had previously accessed. At Devoxx France 2018, Simon Ritter, then Deputy CTO at Azul Systems and a long-time Java evangelist, presented "JDK 9 Mission Accomplished What Next For Java". His talk provided an overview of JDK 9, discussed migration impacts, explained the new OpenJDK development cadence, and looked at future Java features.

Simon began by highlighting the sheer number of features and changes in JDK 9, with JPMS being the centerpiece. Modularity aimed to improve scalability, security (by encapsulating internal APIs), and performance, and to allow developers to create custom JREs containing only the modules their application needed. He explained how JPMS introduced concepts like module descriptors (module-info.java), requires (to declare dependencies on other modules), and exports (to make packages publicly available).

Impact of JDK 9 and Migration Challenges

Migrating applications from earlier Java versions to JDK 9 presented several challenges, primarily due to encapsulation. Code relying on internal APIs like sun.misc.Unsafe would break unless specific command-line flags (like --add-opens or --add-exports) were used as temporary workarounds. Simon Ritter emphasized that these flags were meant to be transitional, encouraging developers to find supported replacements for internal API usage. Another common issue was split packages, where the same package exists in multiple modules (both application modules and JDK modules), which is disallowed by JPMS. Tools like jdeps became essential for analyzing dependencies and identifying potential modularity issues before migration.

Beyond modularity, JDK 9 also introduced other features like the JShell (Java's REPL), improvements to the Process API, an HTTP/2 client (incubator module), and enhancements to the CompletableFuture API.

The New Release Cadence: Java Every Six Months

A crucial part of the presentation focused on Oracle's announced changes to how OpenJDK would be developed and released. Starting with JDK 10 (released March 2018), Java moved to a time-based release model with a new feature release every six months (March and September). Furthermore, Oracle designated specific releases as Long-Term Support (LTS) versions, which would receive public updates for several years. JDK 8 was an LTS release, and JDK 11 (scheduled for September 2018) was slated to be the next LTS. Non-LTS releases (like JDK 9 and 10) would only receive public updates for six months, until the next feature release.

This new cadence meant that businesses and developers needed to decide more frequently whether to stick with an LTS version or keep up with the faster feature releases. Simon explained that Oracle would provide commercial support for their Oracle JDK builds, while OpenJDK builds from Oracle would be free but with the shorter update window for non-LTS versions. Other vendors, like Azul Systems, would also offer OpenJDK builds with their own support options.

What's Next for Java? JDK 10 and Beyond

Simon Ritter then briefly touched upon JDK 10, which had just been released. Its most notable feature was local-variable type inference (using the var keyword), aiming to reduce boilerplate for local variable declarations while maintaining Java's static typing.

Looking further ahead, he discussed several exciting projects incubating within OpenJDK that could shape future Java versions:

  • Project Valhalla: Exploring more advanced value types (inline classes) and generic specialization to improve memory layout and performance for certain data structures.
  • Project Loom: Aiming to bring lightweight, user-mode threads (fibers) and delimited continuations to the JVM, simplifying concurrent programming.
  • Project Panama: Improving the connection between JVM code and native code (interfacing with C/C++ libraries).
  • Project Amber: Focused on smaller, productivity-oriented language features like pattern matching, switch expressions, and raw string literals.
  • Project Metropolis: Investigating the possibility of writing parts of the HotSpot JVM in Java itself.

These projects, Simon concluded, demonstrated Java's continued evolution and commitment to remaining a leading development platform.

Effective Java, Third Edition: Keepin' it Effective (J. Bloch)

Since its initial release in 2001, "Effective Java" has been widely regarded as the definitive guide to best practices for the Java platform. The book's last update was in 2008, coinciding with the release of Java 6. In the decade that followed, the Java platform underwent three major releases, introducing a host of new language and library features that have significantly impacted best practices. At Devoxx France 2018, Joshua Bloch, the author himself, presented "Effective Java, Third Edition: Keepin' it Effective," highlighting key updates from the newly released third edition, with a particular focus on streams and lambdas. The third edition boasts a new chapter, fourteen new items, and extensive revisions to existing content, ensuring its continued relevance for Java developers.

Joshua began by reflecting on the book's history, noting the first edition's publication in 2001. The second edition was primarily driven by the significant additions in Java 5, such as generics, enums, annotations, and varargs. The landscape of Java has continued to evolve, with Java 7, 8, and 9 bringing features like try-with-resources, lambdas, streams, the Date and Time API, and the Java Platform Module System (JPMS). These advancements necessitated a comprehensive update to "Effective Java."

Lambdas and Streams: A Paradigm Shift

A significant portion of Joshua Bloch's talk, and indeed the third edition, is dedicated to the effective use of lambdas and streams, introduced in Java 8. He emphasized that while these features can make code more concise and expressive, they are not a silver bullet and should be used judiciously. One key piece of advice was to prefer side-effect-free functions in streams. Streams are powerful for transforming sequences of data, but introducing side effects (like modifying external state) within stream operations, particularly in forEach blocks that do more than simple presentation, can lead to code that is difficult to understand, debug, and parallelize. Joshua illustrated this with an example of processing a frequency map of words, showing how an imperative approach with a loop might be clearer than a forEach with side effects, but a pure stream-based solution using collectors is often even better.

He also cautioned against overusing streams, stating that streams aren't always the best API for the job. For tasks that are inherently iterative or involve complex control flow that doesn't map well to stream operations (like map, filter, reduce), traditional loops might still be more readable and maintainable. The decision should be based on clarity and what best expresses the programmer's intent. Helper methods can often make stream pipelines more readable by giving descriptive names to complex lambda expressions.

Collection Processing and API Design

Joshua delved into how lambdas impact API design, particularly with methods that operate on collections. He highlighted the removeIf method added to the Collection interface in Java 8 as a prime example of using lambdas to make APIs more flexible. Previously, conditionally removing elements from a collection often required explicit iteration and manual removal, which could be verbose and error-prone. removeIf accepts a predicate, allowing for concise and expressive removal logic.

Another important point was to use java.util.function interfaces for functional parameters. Instead of defining custom functional interfaces, developers should leverage the standard ones provided by the Java platform (like Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier) whenever possible. This promotes interoperability and reduces the cognitive load on users of the API. However, he noted that custom functional interfaces are still appropriate if none of the standard ones fit, if a more descriptive name is needed, or if a contract beyond what the standard interface provides is required.

The Power and Perils of Parallel Streams

The presentation also touched upon parallel streams. Joshua Bloch warned that while parallel() can offer significant performance improvements for certain computations, it's an optimization that should be approached with caution. It's not a magic bullet for making all stream operations faster and can even degrade performance or lead to incorrect results if misused, especially with stateful lambdas or when the overhead of parallelization outweighs the benefits for small datasets or non-CPU-bound tasks. He showed an example of calculating prime numbers where parallel streams provided a near-optimal speedup on a multi-core machine, but emphasized that such scenarios are not always the norm. The advice was to measure performance before and after applying parallel() and to ensure the stream operations are genuinely parallelizable.

Joshua concluded by reiterating that Java has become a more complex, multi-paradigm language. The key to "keeping it effective" is not just knowing how to use the new features, but understanding when and why to use them, always prioritizing clarity and maintainability.

From Mutualism to Open Source: A MAIF Case Study (A. Delègue, M. Ancelin, F. Desmier)

When a company's leadership decides to diversify activities and transform into a service platform, a fundamental rethinking of its information system is often required. At Devoxx France 2018, Alexandre Delègue, Mathieu Ancelin, and François Desmier from MAIF, a French mutual insurance company, shared their journey in "Du mutualisme à l'Open Source" (From Mutualism to Open Source). Over the preceding year and a half, they had conceived and implemented a suite of methodologies, practices, and technical solutions to support new, innovative products with a competitive time-to-market and controlled costs. This initiative, undertaken within a large regional enterprise, embraced the freedom to experiment, discard solutions if necessary, while still valuing legacy systems and empowering developers.

The presentation detailed the stages of this "rupture," the methodologies employed, new ways of working, and the architectural patterns used. A key part of their story was the creation of a custom suite of tools when existing market solutions didn't fit their specific use cases, challenging the notion that "the Netflix stack isn't for everyone." Their agenda included discussing their custom reverse-proxy, API gateway, data ingestion solutions, feature flipping, and A/B testing capabilities.

The Genesis: A Need for Transformation

Mathieu Ancelin began by explaining the context: MAIF, like many established companies, needed to adapt to the digital era and the platform economy. The traditional V-model of development was too slow for the rapid innovation required. They needed to move towards a more agile, microservices-oriented architecture that could support new digital services quickly and efficiently. This led to the creation of a new, independent IT branch within MAIF, nicknamed "the speedboat" to their existing "ocean liner" IT system, tasked with building this new service platform.

Building "Otoroshi": A Unified Gateway

A central piece of their new infrastructure is a tool they developed and open-sourced called "Otoroshi" (Japanese for "terrifying ogre," often depicted as a guardian). Otoroshi serves as a versatile gateway, acting as a reverse proxy, API gateway, and microservice gateway. François Desmier explained that they needed a solution that was highly configurable, developer-friendly, and could handle diverse requirements like canary releasing, A/B testing, fault injection, and robust security (API key management, JWT verification, LDAP integration). Built with Scala and Akka, Otoroshi is designed for high performance and resilience. It allows developers to manage their services' exposure, security policies, and routing rules through a user interface or an API, promoting autonomy.

Another component they highlighted was "Daïkoku," a portal for managing and discovering APIs exposed through Otoroshi, facilitating their consumption by internal and potentially external developers.

Embracing Open Source and InnerSource

A significant theme of the talk was MAIF's shift towards embracing open source, not just as consumers but as contributors and creators. Alexandre Delègue discussed how this cultural change was crucial. By open-sourcing tools like Otoroshi, Daïkoku, and others (like "Izबर्ग" for data ingestion and "Nøshows" for feature flipping and A/B testing), MAIF aimed to give back to the community, attract talent, and foster a culture of quality and collaboration. They also adopted an "InnerSource" model, encouraging internal teams to contribute to these shared tools, breaking down silos and promoting shared ownership.

This journey involved adopting agile methodologies, DevOps practices, and a "you build it, you run it" philosophy, empowering development teams with more responsibility and autonomy. They emphasized the importance of a "platform team" that provides the tools and infrastructure, enabling product teams to focus on delivering business value.

Results and Future

The speakers reported significant improvements in their ability to launch new services and iterate quickly. The new platform, built on these open and custom tools, allowed them to innovate at a much faster pace. They concluded by inviting the audience to explore their open-source projects on GitHub and to consider joining their efforts, as they continue to build out their innovative service platform.

Java 9 Security Enhancements in Practice (M. Toshev)

Java 9, beyond its flagship feature, the Java Platform Module System (JPMS), introduced a range of valuable security enhancements. At Devoxx France 2018, Miroslav Toshev, a Java developer, presented "Java 9 security enhancements in practice," offering a practical look at these new features. His session aimed to demonstrate these enhancements through examples, building upon the foundational knowledge of TLS support in JDK 8, and to discuss the interplay between these security features and the new module system. The new security additions included Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), extensions to the TLS negotiation process (like ALPN), and default PKCS12 keystores, among others.

Miroslav began by contextualizing his talk with previous sessions on JDK 9 and Java security vulnerabilities, positioning his presentation as an extension focusing specifically on the new security capabilities in Java 9. He structured his talk around building modules for a simple banking application server to showcase these features.

Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)

A key enhancement discussed was the introduction of Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) support. DTLS provides communication security for datagram protocols like UDP, which, unlike TCP, do not inherently provide reliable or ordered delivery. Miroslav explained that DTLS is crucial for securing applications that rely on UDP, such as streaming media, online gaming, and VoIP services like SIP (Session Initiation Protocol). He demonstrated how to get started with DTLS in Java 9 by building a simple SIP module for his example banking application, showcasing the new APIs available for establishing secure datagram-based communication. This involved using SSLContext configured for DTLS and working with SSLEngine to handle the DTLS handshake and data encryption/decryption over UDP.

Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN)

Another significant addition covered was the support for Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN). ALPN is a TLS extension that allows the application layer to negotiate which protocol should be handled over a secure connection. This is particularly useful in scenarios where multiple application protocols might be served over the same TLS port, such as HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1. Miroslav Toshev illustrated how to leverage ALPN for protocol negotiation by creating an XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol) module. He showed how the SSLEngine and SSLParameters in Java 9 can be configured to specify the list of application protocols the client or server supports, and how to retrieve the negotiated protocol after the TLS handshake. This allows for more efficient and standardized protocol selection over secure channels.

Other Security Improvements

Beyond DTLS and ALPN, Miroslav touched upon several other security enhancements in Java 9:

  • Default PKCS12 Keystores: Java 9 transitioned the default keystore format from JKS (Java KeyStore) to PKCS12. PKCS12 is an industry-standard format, more widely supported by other tools and languages, offering better interoperability. While JKS is still supported, new keystores will default to PKCS12.
  • OCSP Stapling for TLS: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) stapling was enabled by default for TLS server certificates, improving the performance and reliability of checking certificate revocation status.
  • SHA-3 Hash Algorithms: Support for the SHA-3 family of hash algorithms was added, providing more modern and secure hashing options.
  • Leveraging CPU Instructions for GHASH and RSA: Java 9 was enhanced to utilize specific CPU instructions for accelerating GHASH (used in AES-GCM cipher suites) and RSA operations, leading to performance improvements in cryptographic computations on supported hardware.

Miroslav Toshev concluded by emphasizing that these enhancements, along with the modularity provided by JPMS, contribute to making Java a more secure and robust platform. He encouraged developers to explore these new features to build more secure applications.

How a Chatbot and One Person Support 10,000 Daily Users (G. De Miollis, T. Gloague)

Customer support can be a significant challenge, especially for applications with a large user base. At Devoxx France 2018, Guillaume De Miollis and Thibault Gloague from Pictarine shared their experience in "How a chatbot and 1 person support 10,000 daily users." Pictarine's application, which had a million downloads and processed 50 million printed photos, faced the daunting task of supporting 10,000 daily active users with a very small support team. Their solution involved leveraging Api.ai (now Dialogflow) to build a chatbot that could handle a significant portion of user queries, allowing a single human agent to manage the rest.

The presentation focused on the practical aspects of chatbot implementation, particularly the training process, custom tooling beyond Dialogflow, methods for improving response reliability, and the insights gained about their product through this endeavor.

The Challenge: Scaling Support

Thibault Gloague began by outlining the problem: a year prior, Pictarine's support system was struggling under the load of 10,000 daily users and a high volume of photo prints. The conventional approach of hiring more support agents was not scalable or cost-effective for them. They needed a way to automate responses to common questions and free up human agents for more complex issues. This led them to explore chatbots.

Implementing and Training the Chatbot with Dialogflow

Pictarine chose Api.ai/Dialogflow as their chatbot platform. Guillaume De Miollis explained the initial setup, which involved defining "intents" – the user's intention behind a query – and "entities" – key pieces of information within the query (like dates, order numbers, etc.). The core of their success, however, lay in the continuous training of the chatbot.

The training process involved analyzing user messages that the bot couldn't understand or answered incorrectly. These "failed" interactions were reviewed daily. If a user's phrasing for an existing intent wasn't recognized, that phrasing was added to the intent's training phrases. If a new, legitimate question emerged that the bot couldn't answer, a new intent would be created. This iterative process was crucial for improving the bot's accuracy and coverage over time. They emphasized that training is not a one-time setup but an ongoing effort.

Beyond Dialogflow: Custom Tooling and Workflow

While Dialogflow provided the core NLP and intent matching, Pictarine built custom tools to enhance their support workflow. They developed an internal dashboard that integrated with Dialogflow and their customer support platform (Intercom). This dashboard allowed their single human support agent, Megan, to:

  • See conversations where the bot failed or where the user explicitly requested human help.
  • Easily reclassify misunderstood user utterances to the correct intent, feeding this back into Dialogflow's training.
  • Quickly create new intents or add training phrases based on emerging user queries.
  • Access user context (like order history or app version) alongside the conversation to provide faster, more personalized human support when needed.

This tight integration between the chatbot, custom tools, and the human agent was key to their efficiency. The bot handled the majority of repetitive questions (around 90% of conversations were fully automated), and the custom dashboard streamlined the process for the human agent to manage exceptions and continuously improve the bot.

Lessons Learned and Insights Gained

The speakers shared several lessons from their year-long experience. One crucial learning was the importance of managing user expectations; making it clear that users are interacting with a bot and providing an easy way to escalate to a human is important. They also discovered unexpected insights about their product. For example, by analyzing the questions users asked the bot, they identified confusing aspects of their application интерфейс or missing features that were causing friction. This feedback loop helped them improve not just their support, but their product itself.

They also humorously recounted an incident where their chatbot and another bot got stuck in a loop, texting each other repeatedly, highlighting the need to consider edge cases and implement safeguards. Ultimately, their chatbot-assisted support model allowed them to handle a massive user load effectively, maintain high user satisfaction, and gain valuable product insights, all with a remarkably small human support footprint.

gRPC: High-Frequency Exchanges (D. Caramelo, C. Sistare)

Microservice architectures, while popular and offering benefits like modularity and independent scaling, can introduce challenges related to inter-service communication. Increased network traffic between services can degrade response times, especially when relying on traditional HTTP/REST connections. At Devoxx France 2018, David Caramelo and Carles Sistare from Auguri, a mobile data platform startup, presented their experiences with gRPC as a solution for optimizing this network traffic in their talk, "gRPC, échanges à haute fréquence !" (gRPC, high-frequency exchanges!). Their goal was to re-examine the fundamentals of gRPC, highlight its optimization features, and explain why it can be significantly faster and more efficient than alternatives for high-frequency inter-service communication.

David and Carles began by introducing themselves and their work at Auguri, where they dealt with significant volumes of data and therefore needed efficient communication protocols. Carles Sistare was a co-founder and a committer to projects like kafka-node and had created grpc-promise to simplify working with gRPC in Node.js environments.

Why Not Just Stick with HTTP/REST?

The presentation first addressed the limitations of traditional HTTP/1.1 with JSON for microservices. Key issues highlighted included:

  • Verbosity of JSON: JSON is text-based and can be verbose, leading to larger message sizes.
  • Performance of HTTP/1.1: HTTP/1.1 often involves multiple TCP connections or head-of-line blocking, which can limit throughput.
  • Lack of Strong Typing/Contract: While tools like Swagger/OpenAPI can define REST API contracts, they are often an afterthought, and enforcement can be inconsistent.

Introducing gRPC

gRPC, an open-source Remote Procedure Call framework developed by Google, was presented as a compelling alternative. Its core components and advantages were detailed:

  • Protocol Buffers (Protobuf): gRPC uses Protocol Buffers by default as its Interface Definition Language (IDL) and for message serialization. Protobufs are a language-agnostic, platform-neutral, extensible mechanism for serializing structured data. They offer a compact binary format, which is much more efficient than JSON in terms of size and parsing speed. Defining services and messages in .proto files generates client and server stub code in various languages, ensuring a strong contract.
  • HTTP/2: gRPC leverages HTTP/2 as its transport protocol. HTTP/2 brings several key improvements over HTTP/1.1, including:
    • Multiplexing: Allows multiple requests and responses to be sent concurrently over a single TCP connection, eliminating head-of-line blocking at the connection level.
    • Binary Framing: HTTP/2 uses binary framing, which is more efficient to parse than text-based HTTP/1.1.
    • Header Compression (HPACK): Reduces the overhead of HTTP headers.
    • Server Push: Allows servers to proactively send resources to clients.
    • Streaming: HTTP/2 natively supports bidirectional streaming, allowing for more flexible communication patterns beyond simple request-response. gRPC makes extensive use of this for unary calls, server-side streaming, client-side streaming, and bidirectional streaming.

Practical Benefits and Use Cases

David Caramelo and Carles Sistare shared their practical experiences, noting the significant performance gains they observed by switching from REST/JSON to gRPC for inter-service communication within their platform. They highlighted reduced latency and lower CPU usage due to efficient serialization and the benefits of HTTP/2. The strong contract enforcement through Protobuf definitions also reduced integration issues between services developed by different teams or in different languages.

They also touched upon tooling, such as code generation from .proto files, and how this simplifies development. The ability to use various streaming modes offered by gRPC provided them with flexibility in designing their communication patterns. For example, client-side streaming could be used for ingesting large datasets, while bidirectional streaming could facilitate real-time, interactive communication.

Considerations

While advocating for gRPC, the speakers also implicitly acknowledged the learning curve and the need for a different mindset compared to traditional REST APIs. The ecosystem around gRPC, while growing rapidly, might also require different approaches for things like load balancing, discovery, and observability compared to more established HTTP/1.1 infrastructures, though many solutions now exist (e.g., using service meshes like Istio or Linkerd which have first-class gRPC support).

The talk concluded by reiterating that for high-frequency, performance-sensitive inter-service communication, gRPC offers a compelling set of features and advantages that can lead to more efficient and robust microservice architectures.

From a French Monolith to a Worldwide Platform: A Human Story (S. Chollet, S. Kahlouch)

In September 2016, Dailymotion, a well-known video-sharing platform, began a significant transformation. The company's strategy shifted towards premium content, necessitating a radical and rapid product overhaul. This led to the decision to migrate from their existing PHP monolith, based in a single datacenter, to a geo-distributed, Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) utilizing GraphQL. At Devoxx France 2018, Samuel Chollet (Engineering Manager) and Smaïne Kahlouch (Lead Infrastructure Developer) from Dailymotion presented "From a french monolith to a worldwide platform a human story." They shared their journey, the organizational impact of adopting SOA, their use of CNCF technologies, and the open-source bricks they created along the way.

A year into this transformation, Dailymotion's new product was available globally, with four Kubernetes clusters (a mix of cloud provider and on-premise) distributed worldwide, orchestrating over 1,500 containers and handling over 1,000 requests per second.

The Imperative for Change

Smaïne Kahlouch began by outlining the reasons behind this massive undertaking. The existing monolithic PHP application had several limitations:

  • Scalability issues: Scaling a monolith is often difficult and inefficient.
  • Slow development cycles: Deploying new features or making changes to a large monolith can be slow and risky.
  • Technological constraints: The existing stack made it hard to adopt newer technologies and attract talent.
  • Resilience: A single point of failure in the monolith could impact the entire platform.

The shift to a premium content strategy required a more agile, resilient, and scalable platform.

The Human and Organizational Transformation

Samuel Chollet emphasized that this was not just a technical migration but a profound human and organizational one. Moving to an SOA model required changes in team structures, responsibilities, and culture. They adopted a "you build it, you run it" philosophy, empowering teams with ownership of their services from development through to production. This necessitated new skills, new ways of collaborating, and a shift towards a DevOps culture. Communication and training were crucial to navigate this transition. They also had to manage the "cohabitation" of the old monolithic platform and the new microservices architecture during the migration period.

Technological Choices: Kubernetes, GraphQL, and CNCF Landscape

The new Dailymotion platform heavily leveraged technologies from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) ecosystem.

  • Kubernetes was chosen for container orchestration, providing scalability, resilience, and portability across different environments (cloud and on-premise). Smaïne detailed their experience setting up and managing Kubernetes clusters at scale, including challenges related to networking, storage, and monitoring in a geo-distributed setup.
  • GraphQL was adopted as the API query language for the frontend, sitting in front of their backend microservices. This allowed client applications to request exactly the data they needed in a single request, reducing over-fetching and under-fetching of data, which was a significant improvement for mobile and web performance. The GraphQL layer acted as an aggregation point, fetching data from various downstream microservices.
  • gRPC was used for communication between the GraphQL gateway and the backend microservices, chosen for its performance and efficiency.
  • Other CNCF tools like Prometheus for monitoring and Fluentd for logging were integral to their observability stack.

Building and Open-Sourcing Tools

During this journey, the Dailymotion team developed several tools to address specific needs and later open-sourced them. This included solutions for managing GraphQL schemas, tools for Kubernetes deployment and management, and potentially libraries to facilitate their specific microservice patterns. Sharing these tools was part of their commitment to the open-source community and a way to attract talent.

Challenges and Learnings

The speakers were candid about the challenges encountered, including incidents in production and the steep learning curve associated with some of the new technologies. They shared lessons learned regarding:

  • The importance of robust monitoring and alerting from day one.
  • The complexities of managing stateful applications in Kubernetes.
  • The cultural shift required to truly embrace DevOps and microservices.
  • The benefits of a gradual migration strategy versus a big-bang approach.

Despite the hurdles, the transformation was a success, enabling Dailymotion to launch its new global platform, innovate faster, and scale more effectively. The story highlighted that such a large-scale migration is as much about people and process as it is about technology.

What If Mario Were a UX Designer? (A. Nemery, S. Colmon)

Have you ever felt frustrated playing a video game due to unintuitive controls, or bored by lengthy loading screens? Do you find game inventories often poorly designed? If so, you've experienced user experience (UX) problems in your gaming life. At Devoxx France 2018, Anthony Nemery and Sylvain Colmon presented "Et si Mario était UX designer" (What if Mario was a UX designer?), offering a fresh perspective on UX through concrete examples from popular video games. Their talk explored essential elements that contribute to a good user experience, drawing parallels between usability in software and playability in games, from retro classics to modern blockbusters.

The premise was that the principles that make a game fun and engaging are often the same principles that make a software application intuitive and effective. The Super Mario saga, for instance, is praised for its simplicity and fun, begging the question of its "magic recipe."

Core UX Principles Through a Gaming Lens

Anthony and Sylvain used iconic game examples to illustrate fundamental UX concepts:

  • Affordance and Signifiers: Good UX makes it clear what users can do and how to do it. In games, this translates to intuitive controls and clear visual cues. For example, a glowing item might signify it can be picked up, or a cracked wall might suggest it can be broken. They contrasted games with clear affordances (like the early Mario games where jumping on enemies is a core, easily understood mechanic) with those that might have obscure or inconsistent controls, leading to player frustration.
  • Feedback: Users need to know if their actions have been successful or if the system is processing something. Games provide constant feedback: sound effects for actions, visual confirmation when an item is collected, or controller vibration. The talk showed examples of effective feedback (e.g., a satisfying "thwomp" sound) versus poor feedback (e.g., unclear if a button press registered).
  • Learnability and Onboarding: A good UX allows users to learn how to use an application (or play a game) quickly and easily. Many games excel at "invisible tutorials," where the game mechanics are taught through gameplay itself, rather than lengthy text instructions. The first level of Super Mario Bros. is a masterclass in this, teaching jumping, breaking blocks, and dealing with enemies without a single line of text. This contrasts with applications or games that overwhelm new users with too much information upfront.
  • Consistency: Users expect similar elements to behave in similar ways. In games, if one type of switch opens doors, other similar-looking switches should also open doors. Inconsistent design in applications (e.g., different icons for the same action on different screens) leads to confusion, just as it does in games.
  • Error Prevention and Recovery: Good UX design tries to prevent users from making errors and provides easy ways to recover if they do. Games often use features like undo (e.g., rewinding time in some puzzle games), clear warnings before critical actions (like deleting a save file), or forgiving mechanics that don't punish minor mistakes too harshly.
  • User Control and Freedom: Users should feel in control and be able to navigate and exit processes easily. Games provide pause menus, options to quit, and generally allow players to explore at their own pace (within the game's structure). Applications that trap users in long wizards or make it hard to cancel operations violate this principle.

The "Gamer Experience" as UX Inspiration

The speakers argued that developers and designers could learn a lot by considering the "gamer experience." Game designers are masters at engaging users, managing cognitive load, and creating intuitive interfaces under the pressure of keeping players entertained and immersed. Frustration due to poor game design (clunky controls, confusing menus, unfair difficulty spikes often rooted in UX issues) leads to players abandoning the game – much like users might abandon a poorly designed application.

Anthony Nemery and Sylvain Colmon encouraged the audience to re-evaluate user experience from this more playful and often more innovative perspective, suggesting that the line between good usability and good "playability" is very thin indeed. They also recommended books like Steve Krug's "Don't Make Me Think" as foundational UX texts.

Ending Dependency Management Problems with Gradle (C. Champeau)

Dependency management is a common source of frustration for developers. Issues like classpath conflicts from different versions of the same library, unintended transitive dependencies due to incorrect metadata on Maven Central, ensuring compatibility with specific framework versions like Spring 5, or managing semantic versioning upgrades are all too frequent. Enterprises face even more complex challenges, such as ensuring that projects only depend on QA-validated versions, freezing versions for reproducible builds, or blacklisting buggy library versions. At Devoxx France 2018, Cédric Champeau from Gradle Inc. presented "En finir avec les problèmes de gestion de dépendances" (Ending dependency management problems).

His talk focused on how Gradle, particularly with features introduced up to version 5, aimed to solve these long-standing issues. While Gradle had historically supported metadata from Maven (pom.xml) and Ivy (ivy.xml), a new Gradle-specific metadata format was introduced, designed to support variants and tackle these problems in a more open environment, catering not just to Java but also to native development (C++, Swift, etc.).

The Problems with Traditional Dependency Management

Cédric began by acknowledging the pervasive nature of dependency hell. He highlighted common pain points:

  • Transitive dependency conflicts: When different direct dependencies bring in incompatible versions of the same transitive library (e.g., Guava, Jackson).
  • Incorrect metadata: POM files on Maven Central often contain errors, such as declaring compile-time dependencies that are actually only needed for testing, or omitting necessary transitive dependencies.
  • Lack of semantic versioning enforcement: Upgrading a library from 1.0.2 to 2.0.4 might be allowed by the build tool even if it's a major breaking change, because the tool doesn't inherently understand semantic versioning rules defined by the library author.
  • Inability to express rich dependency constraints: Simple version ranges are often not enough to express complex compatibility rules or to select different variants of a library (e.g., a Java 8 vs. Java 11 compatible jar, or a full vs. lite version).

Gradle's Approach: Rich Metadata and Variant Awareness

Gradle's solution revolves around a richer metadata format and a more sophisticated dependency resolution engine. Key concepts include:

  • Gradle Module Metadata (.module file): This new JSON-based format allows library publishers to declare much richer information about their components than what's possible with POM files. This includes:
    • Variants: Libraries can declare different "variants" of themselves, for example, one compiled with Java 8 and another with Java 11, or variants with different sets of optional features. Gradle can then select the most appropriate variant based on the consumer's context.
    • Capabilities: Modules can declare abstract "capabilities" they provide (e.g., "JSON parsing") and which other modules provide the same capability, allowing Gradle to resolve conflicts at a capability level.
    • Rich Version Constraints: More expressive ways to define version compatibility, including strict versions, preferred versions, and rejected versions.
    • Dependency Constraints: The ability for consumers to define constraints on transitive dependencies (e.g., "my project must use Guava version X, regardless of what my direct dependencies request").
  • Component Metadata Rules: For libraries that haven't published Gradle Module Metadata, consumers can define client-side rules to correct or augment existing Maven/Ivy metadata. This allows users to fix issues with incorrect POMs without waiting for the library author to republish.
  • Attributes: A system for matching consumer requirements with producer capabilities through key-value attributes (e.g., org.gradle.jvm.version=11, org.gradle.usage=java-runtime). This is how variant selection works.

Practical Implications and Benefits

Cédric Champeau demonstrated how these features could solve common dependency problems. For instance, by declaring variants, a library can offer both a Java 8 and a Java 11 jar, and Gradle will automatically pick the right one based on the consumer project's Java version. If a library's POM incorrectly pulls in a test dependency as a compile dependency, a component metadata rule can fix this.

He also highlighted features like available-at for publishing metadata independently of artifacts (useful for platforms or Bill of Materials - BOMs), and the concept of dependency locking to ensure reproducible builds by pinning dynamic or range-based versions to specific resolved versions.

The overarching goal is to shift towards a world where library metadata is more accurate and expressive, allowing build tools like Gradle to make smarter decisions and significantly reduce the pain of dependency management. Cédric encouraged library authors to start publishing Gradle Module Metadata and for consumers to leverage these new capabilities to improve their build reliability and maintainability. He pointed out that popular plugins like those from Spring and Netflix for dependency management could simplify their codebase significantly by leveraging Gradle's native capabilities.

Modernizing Monoliths with Docker, Kubernetes, and Istio

At Devoxx France 2018, David Gageot delivered a talk titled Docker, Kubernetes et Istio, c'est utile pour mon monolithe?, available on YouTube. Focusing on legacy monolithic applications, Gageot demonstrated how Docker, Kubernetes, and Istio can enhance deployment, security, and observability without modifying a single line of code. Using the Java-based Pet Store application, he showcased practical techniques like containerization, blue-green deployments, and service mesh capabilities. This session empowers developers to modernize monoliths incrementally, leveraging cloud-native tools for resilience and scalability.

Who Is David Gageot?

David Gageot, a seasoned developer, humorously set the stage by noting that 80% of developers work on monoliths, not microservices. His experience with real-world production systems informs his pragmatic approach. At Devoxx, he aimed to show how containerization and orchestration tools can breathe new life into legacy applications. Using live demos and the Pet Store—a classic Java EE app originally built by Sun Microsystems and later updated by Antonio Goncalves—Gageot illustrated how to evolve monoliths without rewriting them, assuming the original developers are long gone.

Why Containers for Monoliths?

Gageot began by addressing the misconception that Docker and Kubernetes are only for microservices. Monoliths, often complex and hard to modify, benefit from containerization’s isolation and portability. Docker packages applications with their dependencies, ensuring consistency across environments. Kubernetes orchestrates these containers across a cluster, abstracting infrastructure details like IP addresses or server names. Istio, a service mesh, adds intelligent network management, enabling features like secure communication and traffic routing. Together, these tools simplify upgrades, cloud deployments, and monitoring for monoliths.

Containerizing the Pet Store

Gageot chose the Pet Store, a monolithic Java EE application with a web interface, business logic, and database, to demonstrate containerization. He built a Docker image using a multi-stage Dockerfile. The first stage, based on a Maven image, fetched the Pet Store source from GitHub and built a WAR file using mvn package. The second stage, based on a lightweight JBoss WildFly image, copied the WAR file for runtime, minimizing the final image’s size and attack surface. This approach separates build and runtime environments, enhancing security and efficiency.

Deploying with Kubernetes

To run the Pet Store on a Kubernetes cluster, Gageot defined two YAML manifests: a Deployment and a Service. The Deployment specified the Docker image and metadata like labels (e.g., app name, version), allowing Kubernetes to manage replicas and updates. The Service exposed the application on port 8080, enabling external access. Using kubectl apply, he deployed these manifests to a single-node cluster on his laptop, connecting via localhost:8080. Kubernetes’ control loops ensured the desired state, automatically restarting containers if they failed, as shown when Gageot killed a pod and watched it recover.

Enhancing with a Sidecar Facade

To improve the Pet Store without altering its code, Gageot introduced a sidecar pattern. He added an Nginx container alongside the application in the same Kubernetes pod, acting as a reverse proxy. Configured to enable gzip compression, serve a 404 page, and rewrite URLs (e.g., removing /site/petcare), this facade improved user experience externally. The Service was updated to route traffic to Nginx’s port 80. This pattern, common in cloud-native setups, allows cosmetic and functional enhancements without touching the monolith, running both containers on the same node for efficiency.

Istio’s Power: Service Mesh for Monoliths

Gageot then introduced Istio, a service mesh that extends Kubernetes with advanced networking. By injecting an Envoy proxy sidecar into each pod, Istio intercepts all traffic, enabling features like automatic HTTPS between services, traffic monitoring, and intelligent routing. For the Pet Store, this meant secure communication without modifying Java code. Istio’s certificate authority generated TLS certificates, ensuring encrypted traffic across the cluster. Gageot emphasized its “plug-and-play” nature, ideal for banks or finance where manual HTTPS setup is labor-intensive.

Blue-Green Deployments

To demonstrate blue-green deployment, Gageot deployed a v2 Pet Store with a new stylesheet, running alongside v1. Using Istio’s routing rules, he directed 80% of traffic to v1 and 20% to v2, based on domain names (petstore.example.com vs. dev2.petstore.example.com). He adjusted these weights to 50/50 and 100% v2, monitoring the transition with Istio’s Grafana dashboards. These dashboards, leveraging labels, showed request volumes per version, ensuring no errors during the rollout. Istio’s mirroring feature also allowed testing v2 with real traffic asynchronously, ignoring v2 responses to validate performance.

Evolving to Microservices

Gageot showed how to incrementally extract microservices from the monolith. He created a new service for the Pet Store’s UI, using an Nginx container for static content and a Go-based REST API container. Istio routed /ui/* URLs to this service, while others went to the Pet Store. The Go service fetched data from the monolith’s API, transforming verbose responses into cleaner JSON. This approach “starves” the monolith by redirecting traffic to modern components, evolving the system without rewriting it.

Resilience and Observability

Istio enhanced resilience with features like retries (e.g., retrying failed requests five times), circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures, and rate limiting (e.g., one request per second to the Pet Store). Gageot demonstrated rate limiting, showing 429 errors when exceeding limits. For observability, Istio’s Service Graph visualized service interactions, revealing dependencies and traffic flows. Distributed tracing and metrics in Grafana provided insights into request paths and performance, crucial as monoliths split into services.

Why It Matters

Gageot’s talk proves that Docker, Kubernetes, and Istio aren’t just for microservices. Monoliths gain portability, scalability, and resilience through containerization and orchestration. Istio’s service mesh adds security, observability, and traffic control, enabling blue-green deployments and incremental modernization. Developers can evolve legacy systems without risky rewrites, leveraging open-source tools like Istio, developed by IBM, Google, and the community. This session inspires confidence in modernizing monoliths, one container at a time.

Crafting Soulful Voice Assistants

At Devoxx France 2018, Jean-Philippe Encausse and Alexis Vasseur presented a talk titled Donnez une âme à vos assistants vocaux, available on YouTube. Encausse, creator of the open-source SARAH project, and Vasseur, a functional design expert, explored the art of designing conversational voice assistants. Focusing on ergonomics over technology, they showcased SARAH v5’s Node-RED integration, enabling non-technical users to craft dialogues. This session offers developers and designers a blueprint for creating engaging, human-like voice interactions.

Who Are Encausse and Vasseur?

Jean-Philippe Encausse, a technical expert, launched SARAH in 2013, a platform for home automation via voice. His work on chatbots for brands like Sephora and Salesforce informs his insights. Alexis Vasseur, with a functional focus, complements Encausse by emphasizing user experience. Their talk blended technical and design perspectives, using SARAH v5—rewritten with IBM’s Node-RED—to demonstrate how to build conversational flows as “Lego bricks.” They aimed to make voice assistants intuitive, leveraging open-source tools to prioritize ergonomics.

The Rise of Voice Assistants

Encausse traced the evolution of conversational interfaces, comparing voice assistants to the iPhone’s ergonomic revolution. Since 2016, platforms like Facebook Messenger (2.2 billion users) and WeChat have popularized chatbots, while voice assistants like Google Home and Alexa have gone mainstream. Unlike mobile apps, voice interfaces lack screens, relying on speech and imagination. This shift demands new design paradigms, as users interact via natural language, expecting fluid conversations. The challenge is creating assistants that feel human, not robotic, across diverse channels.

SARAH v5: Designing Conversations with Node-RED

SARAH v5, fully open-source, uses Node-RED’s graphical interface to let functional designers build conversation flows without coding. Encausse demonstrated a typical flow: a user’s message is sent to Microsoft’s Bot Framework, then to Google’s Dialogflow for intent detection (e.g., booking a store appointment). Node-RED routes responses based on intent, sending text or speech back to the user’s device. Developers can add custom JavaScript “bricks” for logic, while non-technical users tweak dialogues via forms. This modular approach supports GAFAM technologies, ensuring compatibility.

Defining a Voice Assistant’s Purpose

Vasseur emphasized starting with user observation. Voice assistants integrate into daily life, like cooking or commuting, offering new interaction patterns. They serve two goals: efficiency (e.g., booking a pizza in one sentence) or personalization (e.g., a Direct Energie chatbot coaching users to save electricity). Clear, explicit promises are crucial—Sephora’s assistant helps reduce energy use, not provide weather updates. This clarity prevents user frustration, ensuring the assistant’s purpose aligns with real needs.

Crafting a Personality

Giving an assistant “soul” means defining its personality. Vasseur described creating a fictional character, like Gaius, a serpent-themed train assistant. Gaius is polite, slightly old-fashioned (using “sapristi”), and sensitive but helpful. His backstory—he dreamed of driving trains but lacks hands—adds depth, surfacing in small talk. Personality shapes tone (formal for customer complaints, casual for millennials), language (tutoiement vs. vouvoiement), and even avatars (illustrations for fiction, none for Google Assistant to spark imagination).

Voice and Sound Design

Voice defines the assistant’s identity. Options include platform voices (Google Assistant, Alexa), customizable via SSML for pauses and emphasis, or bespoke synthetic voices (e.g., SNCF’s brand voice). Encausse highlighted advanced synthesis like Google’s WaveNet, though limited to English in 2018. Sound design, like BBC’s scripted games with actors or Sephora’s daily beauty podcasts, creates immersive experiences. Jingles, as in Google’s quiz game, evoke TV show vibes, enhancing engagement.

Handling Small Talk and Variants

Assistants must handle “small talk” (e.g., “thank you,” insults) beyond their core service. Encausse leveraged Dialogflow’s pre-trained intents for common queries, customizing responses in spreadsheets for non-developers. To avoid monotony, responses vary—“de rien,” “avec plaisir”—and escalate for repeated inputs (e.g., Gaius teasing after multiple “thanks”). This builds familiarity, making interactions feel alive. For insults, assistants might sulk playfully, reinforcing personality.

Technical Building Blocks

Encausse outlined technical components. Speech-to-text uses GAFAM’s NLP tools (Dialogflow, Amazon Lex), extracting intents and entities (e.g., “book makeup at Sephora Rivoli, June 10, 4 PM”). Keyword spotting (“OK Google”) remains GAFAM-controlled, requiring extensive audio training for custom triggers. Payment systems, like Alexa’s voice-matched purchases, are emerging but immature in Europe. Multimodal interactions (voice plus visuals on TVs) and edge computing (local vision processing via Google’s Vision Kit) are future trends.

Evolving Through Feedback

Assistants evolve via user feedback. Encausse shared Sephora’s case: users asked to “visit the website” vocally, revealing a need for mobile redirects. Analytics from Google, Alexa, or custom tools (e.g., Botmetrics) identify unmet intents, guiding improvements. If an assistant fails, it redirects to human support or web channels to reduce frustration. GDPR compliance is critical, as voice is personal data, requiring careful handling to avoid logging sensitive inputs.

Why It Matters

This talk redefines voice assistants as ergonomic, human-like companions, not just tech. SARAH v5’s Node-RED integration empowers designers to craft engaging dialogues, while technical bricks ensure flexibility. By focusing on personality, sound, and user needs, developers can create assistants that delight, from train schedules to beauty tips. The open-source approach invites community innovation, making voice design accessible. This session inspires building assistants with soul, transforming how we interact with technology.
